docs.title: Wildmeshing Toolkit
docs.text:
Robust, parallel triangle and tetrahedral mesh generation and editing.

The toolkit writes mesh algorithms as local operations — split, collapse, swap, smooth — together with the invariants every operation must keep and the rules that update attributes. It schedules the operations in parallel, checks the invariants, and rolls back any operation that would break them. On this foundation it implements TetWild, TriWild, QSlim, isotropic remeshing, multi-region meshing, topological offsets and more, each callable from the command line, Python and C++ with the same JSON options.

git clone https://github.com/wildmeshing/wildmeshing-toolkit.git
cd wildmeshing-toolkit
python -m pip install .

import wildmeshing as wm

bunny = wm.read_mesh(str(DATA / "bunny.obj"))
outputs, report = wm.tetwild({"input": ["bunny"], "num_threads": 4}, {"bunny": bunny})
print(report["#t"], "tets, max energy", report["max_energy"])
wm.write_mesh("bunny_tets.vtu", outputs["mesh"])

docs.title: Where to go
docs.text:
• Getting started: install, run a first component, and learn the two ways to call one.
  • Tutorials: each component, its key settings, with examples in JSON, Python and C++.
  • Gallery: the components' results, interactive.
  • Reference: every option of every component, the Python API, the C++ API.
  • Concepts: local operations, scheduling, robust geometry, quality.
  • Developer guide: the code, and how to add an operation or a component.

The toolkit is described in Declarative Specification for Unstructured Mesh Editing Algorithms (ACM Transactions on Graphics, SIGGRAPH Asia 2022): see Citing. It is MIT licensed.

docs.title: Component I/O
docs.text:
Every registered component exposes its existing file-oriented entry point and an owning, in-memory interface:

void name(nlohmann::json options);
ComponentResult name(nlohmann::json options, const MeshMap& meshes);

MeshMap is std::map<std::string, MeshData>. ComponentResult is a pair of named output meshes and a JSON report. The memory overload never resolves a selector as a filename, never changes its input meshes, and does not emit mesh, report, log, or debug files. It does not require application, input_dir, or output filenames. Python exposes both interfaces, using plain dictionaries of NumPy arrays for mesh data.

#include <wmtk/io/mesh_io.hpp>
#include <wmtk/components/qslim/qslim.hpp>

wmtk::MeshMap meshes{{"surface", wmtk::io::read_mesh("input.obj")}};
auto [outputs, report] = wmtk::components::qslim::qslim(
    {{"input", "surface"}, {"target_rel", 0.5}}, meshes);
wmtk::io::write_mesh("simplified.vtu", outputs.at("mesh"));

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Build and install in your active environment with python -m pip install -e .. Every enabled component exposes name(options) for the existing file interface and name(options, meshes) for the memory interface. The latter returns (meshes, report). wildmeshing(options) remains compatible; wildmeshing(options, meshes) selects the memory component from options["application"]. Direct component calls do not require application.

import numpy as np
import wildmeshing as wm

surface = {
    "V": np.array([[0., 0., 0.], [1., 0., 0.], [0., 1., 0.]], dtype=np.float64),
    "cells": {
        "triangle": {"connectivity": np.array([[0, 1, 2]], dtype=np.int64)},
    },
}
meshes, report = wm.qslim(
    {"input": "surface", "target_rel": 1.0, "eps_rel": 0.0},
    {"surface": surface},
)
positions = meshes["mesh"]["V"]
# Explicit file I/O is separate from the memory call:
wm.write_mesh("result.msh", meshes["mesh"])
loaded = wm.read_mesh("result.msh")

The dictionary mirrors the C++ data structure:

  • V: an (n, 3) NumPy array. Floating coordinates are promoted to Float64; integer coordinates must convert exactly. Returned positions always use Float64.
  • cells: a dictionary keyed by point, edge, triangle, quad, tetrahedron, prism, or pyramid. Each block contains a two-dimensional integer connectivity array and an optional attributes dictionary. Returned connectivity uses Int64.
  • Optional vertex_attributes and cell attributes map names to {"values": array, "labels": [column_names...]}. Labels may be omitted; a bare array is also accepted as an unlabeled input attribute. Attribute dtypes are Float64, Int64, or UInt8. One-dimensional input attributes become column matrices. Returned fields always contain values and labels.

For example, overlapping region memberships are represented as:

mesh["cells"]["tetrahedron"]["attributes"] = {
    "tags": {
        "values": np.array([[1, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=np.uint8),
        "labels": ["region_a", "region_b"],
    },
}

Only selected dictionary entries are converted and validated. JSON selector arrays retain their order. Inputs may be read-only or strided arrays: the binding copies selected data into owning C++ arrays before computation. Outputs own their NumPy storage and can be passed directly into subsequent memory calls. Connectivity is never truncated from floating point, and Int64 attributes never pass through Float64. Computation releases the Python GIL. Component attribute contracts and the shared readers' and writers' supported formats are the same as in C++.

Run the Python memory tests with python -m unittest discover -s tests/python -p test_memory_io.py, and those of tracking -- histories and wm.Tracking / wm.CurveTracking -- with -p test_tracking.py; they are also included in the wheel tests.

docs.title: MeshData
docs.text:
• V is an owning row-major Float64 matrix with three columns. Pad 2D coordinates with zero.
  • cells[CellType] holds a row-major Int64 connectivity matrix and named attributes. Cell types are point (1 corner), edge (2), triangle (3), quad (4), tetrahedron (4), prism (6), and pyramid (5). Prism/pyramid ordering follows VTK.
  • vertex_attributes and each cell block's attributes map names to MeshAttribute. values is a variant of row-major Float64, Int64, or UInt8 matrices. One row corresponds to a vertex or a row in that cell block's connectivity. Vectors are one-column matrices.
  • MeshAttribute::labels optionally names columns. tags uses a binary UInt8 matrix with one named column per physical/material group, allowing overlapping memberships. Group names are labels of this fixed field, rather than arbitrary extra attribute names.
  • validate() checks geometry, connectivity, and attribute dimensions. Coordinates must be finite. Attributes may contain undefined numerical diagnostics such as NaN. A cell may repeat a vertex: components clean degenerate input cells exactly as their file readers do.

Only top-dimensional connectivity is needed to construct an algorithm's mesh. Explicit lower blocks identify the edges/faces carrying attributes; their row order is independent of internal mesh IDs. Do not use internal edge/face IDs as interchange indices. Exact positions, caches, rollback buffers, and mesh objects are not part of MeshData.

docs.title: Input contracts
docs.text:
Selectors retain their component-specific JSON fields. A single selector is a dictionary key; ordered selector arrays preserve input order and existing input_names / transform semantics. Unselected dictionary entries are not validated. Missing keys and incompatible inputs throw std::runtime_error before computation. Unknown attributes are rejected; this interface does not transfer arbitrary user attributes through topology changes. Geometry-only inputs ("no attributes" below) ignore the fields io::read_mesh attaches to plain geometry files: vertex vid, and triangle uv and normal. A component may accept, and ignore, a field of its own results as well, so that a result can be the next call's input as it is: isotropic_remeshing's vertex_id, whose fixed vertices come from features alone.

Component Mesh selectors Required data qslim input Triangle geometry, no attributes shortest_edge_collapse input Triangle geometry, no attributes isotropic_remeshing input; optional features Triangle geometry, no attributes but its own vertex_id, ignored; features on the rows of input: edges with Int64 edge_id, points with Int64 vertex_id, or Int64 vertex vertex_id (-1 for none) tetwild input; input_edges, input_points Triangle surfaces; optional curve/point geometry, no attributes triwild input; input_points Curve geometry, optional free points, no attributes simwild input; optional envelope for tagged input Surface/curve geometry, or tagged triangle/tet mesh topological_offset input; optional envelope Tagged triangle/tet mesh manifold_extraction input; optional envelope Tagged triangle/tet mesh prismatic_mesh input Tet construction mesh with corr_input_vid and cell region memberships c1_simplification surface_mesh, uv_mesh Surface triangle dofs (Float64, 36 columns), vertex is_cone (UInt8, 1 column); UV triangle geometry tracking none for info and features; transfer: input, optional tet_mesh; volume: optional tet_mesh and output_tet_mesh The history as bytes (option history, not a mesh), and for volume the volume history as bytes (option volume_history). transfer: the triangle surface the history starts from, whose triangle attributes it carries (uv, normal per corner, any other per face), no vertex attributes; the tet mesh the history ends at. volume: the tet meshes the volume history starts and ends at, with their tags if they have them

For tagged inputs, tags on the top-dimensional cells names their regions, such as tag_0. A column labelled ambient is the background, as is a cell without a tag; a mesh without a tags field is all background. Tagged results label their background ambient explicitly; the shared readers and writers infer nothing from an untagged row. Existing exported diagnostics have fixed allowed names in the adapters and may be supplied again. Extra unrelated fields are errors. As on the .msh route, a lower-dimensional block of the envelope's type (triangles in a tet mesh, edges in a triangle mesh) is the envelope, e.g. simwild's EnvelopeSurface; it cannot be combined with an envelope input. Other lower-dimensional blocks are rejected.

The prismatic adapter accepts scalar tag_0 and offset_tag, or the corresponding columns of tags. vid defaults to vertex row IDs; absent labels are derived from input-volume cells and correspondence. corr_input_vid names a source vid, with -1 for no correspondence. Existing construction diagnostics are accepted. Enable save_offset_correspondence and disable offset optimization to obtain construction correspondence for the offset-to-prismatic workflow.

C1's 36 DOF columns flatten its 12-by-3 face matrix in row order. UV vertices use V's first two columns; UV faces correspond to surface face rows. Its unfinished tetrahedral mapping route is unchanged.

docs.title: Results and compatibility
docs.text:
mesh is the primary output key. Components also return their applicable existing secondary geometry under fixed keys:

  • surface: the boundary (triangles in 3D; in 2D -- triwild, 2D simwild -- the boundary edges). Manifold extraction returns its extracted boundary here.
  • edges: simwild's 3D feature edges; isotropic_remeshing's feature edges, with features (its Int64 edge_id, and mesh's Int64 vertex_id, are what its .vtu output holds, an edge block of none where there are none), which can be the next call's features.
  • offset: the offset surface or front; prismatic's classified offset faces.
  • envelope, features, uv, and manifold extraction's 3D input-complex preview input_complex.
  • Prismatic export_input_and_shell adds input_and_shell and its classified offset faces as input_and_shell_offset; with prism_dominant, the report adds that export's input_and_shell_hybrid report, as in its _hybrid.json file.
  • history_input: simwild's, with history_output, the tagged tet mesh its surface history starts from (the file route's <output>_history_input.msh); tetwild's, with volume_history_output, the tet mesh its volume history starts from (its <output>_history_input.msh).
  • history_output: tetwild's, with volume_history_output, the tet mesh its volume history ends at, all of it before the filter (its <output>_history_output.msh); mesh is the part the filter keeps. For simwild the volume history ends at mesh.

For tetwild, triwild, simwild, topological_offset and isotropic_remeshing, surface, edges and offset share the mesh vertex rows: their connectivity indexes the same V, with the same vertex fields, so row i is the same vertex in every one of them, and vertices an output does not reference are kept. This is deliberate -- it maps a boundary vertex to its volume vertex without a search -- at the cost of one vertex array per output. envelope, features, manifold extraction's surface and prismatic's offset faces have vertices of their own.

The exporters' legacy file names map to these keys through one explicit table (io::default_output_keys); an unmapped export or two exports with one key is an error, never a silently dropped output. Reports contain the existing algorithm counts, quality measures, and timings; prismatic reports also contain hybrid and smoothing/remeshing reports. Report values are available without a report filename.

The existing topological-offset driver currently refuses 2D inputs; the memory overload preserves that restriction.

The file-oriented entry points retain existing configurations, relative-path conventions, output filenames, intermediate exports, and report files. The tagged components (simwild, triwild, topological_offset, manifold_extraction) build the same result on both routes: the file route writes its mesh (the envelope stays out of the file) through io::write_mesh, and reads its .msh input through io::read_mesh. An explicit per-call output policy turns off their file observers for memory calls. Component entry points serialize their use of the legacy process-wide loggers, temporarily using console sinks during memory calls and restoring the previous logger afterward.

Component calls do not run concurrently. Every call -- file or memory, from C++ or Python -- holds one process-wide lock for its whole duration, so calls from several threads run one after another; the Python bindings release the GIL, but a second call still waits for the first. Use num_threads for parallelism within a call. Existing algorithm options, filtering, cleaning, and exact-arithmetic decisions are shared between the two routes.

docs.title: Histories
docs.text:
isotropic_remeshing, qslim, shortest_edge_collapse, tetwild and simwild in 3D record the history of their surface with history_output, and triwild the history of its curves, from which tracking rebuilds the map between input and output (see docs/tracking.md). The file route saves it to that file. The memory route writes no file: any non-empty history_output turns the recording on, and the report returns the history as history, the bytes of the file the file route would write -- a nlohmann::json binary value in C++. On the memory route the history starts at the meshes given and ends at the meshes returned. history::write_history(path, bytes) saves the bytes as that file, unchanged, and history::read_history(path) reads them back, as io::write_mesh and io::read_mesh do for a mesh; history::SurfaceHistory::from_bytes and history::CurveHistory::from_bytes load them, and history::face_size(bytes) says which they hold (3 corners a face, or 2). The history file is its own format, not a mesh.

tetwild and simwild in 3D also record the volume around the tracked surface with volume_history_output (which needs history_output). The memory route returns it the same way, as volume_history in the report, the bytes of its file, and writes no file; with it the meshes the volume history names its points by, as output meshes: history_input, where it starts, and tetwild's history_output, the mesh before its filter, where it ends (simwild's ends at mesh). read_history and write_history take a volume history by its header as they take the others; history::VolumeHistory::from_bytes loads it and history::is_volume_history says that bytes are one.

tracking takes the bytes as history on the memory route, where a string is refused, as every memory call refuses to take a name for a file. info returns its report, of a surface or of a curve history. features, on a curve history, returns its feature points in the report: feature_points, pairs of an input vertex and the output vertex it became, -1 for none (an Int64 array of two columns in NumPy). transfer, on a surface history, needs input, the mesh the history starts from -- the history's own parameters name meshes of an earlier call, or files, neither of which the memory route reads -- and returns the output surface as mesh, the carried fields as triangle attributes, per face or, for uv and normal, three values per corner (uv: six columns), with input_face (Int64), the input face each output face comes from. With tet_mesh, the tet mesh the history ends at, it also returns that mesh as tet_mesh with the fields on the rows of its triangle block: a tracked face already there (a face tag) on its row, any other on a row added after them. volume takes the volume history's bytes as volume_history -- a string is refused there too -- and, to sample points near the tracked surface and check where they land, tet_mesh and output_tet_mesh, keys of the meshes given (a producer's history_input, and its mesh or history_output); its report holds what the file route logs (stats, round_trip, regions_kept, ...). map and map_volume, whose points are text files, are refused on the memory route: points are mapped in memory by Tracking, CurveTracking and VolumeTracking (components/tracking/.../tracking.hpp), in Python wm.Tracking, wm.CurveTracking and wm.VolumeTracking.

In Python the history is bytes: the bindings return a report's binary values as bytes, and pass bytes in the options as binary values (pybind11_json alone would make them base64 text). wm.write_history(path, history) and wm.read_history(path) are the two file functions:

outputs, report = wm.isotropic_remeshing(
    {"input": "surface", "history_output": "record"}, {"surface": surface})
wm.write_history("remeshed.wmtkhist", report["history"])  # the file the file route writes
history = wm.read_history("remeshed.wmtkhist")            # the same bytes

t = wm.Tracking(history)                  # the map; wm.Tracking.load(path) from the file
ids, bary = t.to_output(faces, bary)      # int64 (n,), float64 (n, 3): points on the input
faces, bary = t.to_input(ids, bary)       # and back; -1 (and NaN) for a point with no image

A volume history maps the same way, with the surface history it was recorded with and the two meshes, as a memory call returns them:

outputs, report = wm.tetwild(
    {"input": "surface", "history_output": "x", "volume_history_output": "y"}, {"surface": s})
v = wm.VolumeTracking(report["history"], report["volume_history"],
                      outputs["history_input"], outputs["history_output"])
tets, bary = v.to_output(tets, bary)      # int64 (n,), float64 (n, 4): -1 and NaN for no tet
xyz, region = v.map_positions(xyz)        # float64 (n, 3); direction="to_input", regions=...

wm.VolumeTracking(history, volume_history) maps positions only, and wm.VolumeTracking.load(...) takes the four files instead.

wm.CurveTracking does the same for a curve history: segments of the input curve files (n,) and coordinates (n, 2) to two vertices of the output mesh (n, 2), and back, and feature_points(). Ids are (n,) faces or segments, or (n, 3) / (n, 2) vertices on a side named by a mesh's vertices (output_by_vertices, input_by_vertices); warnings=True adds the call's warnings as a third element. Building a map holds the process-wide lock, as its loading logs; mapping releases the GIL and changes nothing -- a VolumeTracking only the operation maps it keeps, under a lock of its own -- so threads may share one object. docs/tracking.md has the details.

docs.title: Shared file utilities
docs.text:
io::read_mesh(path) reads MSH, OBJ, OFF, STL and the existing libigl surface formats. It preserves row identity and isolated vertices; cleaning belongs to component preprocessing. Nonstandard MSH node tags are preserved as zero-based source IDs in vid, unless an explicit vid field is supplied. OBJ polylines retain orientation, and UV/normal values are represented per triangle corner (uv: six columns; normal: nine columns), read only when every face corner references a value. Existing component-specific VTU input remains unchanged; the shared utilities do not add a VTU reader.

io::write_mesh(path, data) writes MSH or delegates VTU output to the existing paraviewo::VTUWriter, without a new serializer or custom VTU metadata. VTU attributes use the existing Float64 representation, with exact numeric conversion required. Attribute labels, two-column fields (which the writer pads), names requiring XML escaping, and differing attribute schemas across cell blocks are rejected. The writer rounds values below 1e-16 in magnitude to zero, as in every component's own VTU output; this is reported as a warning. Use MSH when those fields need to be preserved. MSH fields use reversible scalar splitting with type/shape/label metadata in their data headers. Integer values that cannot be represented exactly by MSH's Float64 field values are rejected. Physical groups retain overlapping memberships. Undefined floating diagnostics are encoded reversibly in MSH metadata. Unsupported cell types, encodings, and unrepresentable data throw rather than being silently dropped.

docs.title: JSON Schemas
docs.text:
Each component's options are published as a JSON Schema, generated from its spec on every build of this site. An editor that knows the schema completes option names, shows their documentation, and flags a misspelled option or a wrong type before the file runs. That matters because most components ignore an option they do not know.

Schema For schemas/wmtk_app.json any wmtk_app file: it picks the component's schema by application schemas/<component>.json one component, e.g. schemas/tetwild.json

docs.title: In a file
docs.text:
Name the schema in the file itself; wmtk_app ignores the $schema key:

{
  "$schema": "https://wildmeshing.github.io/wildmeshing-toolkit/schemas/wmtk_app.json",
  "application": "qslim",
  "input": "Octocat.obj",
  "target_rel": 0.1
}

docs.title: In VS Code
docs.text:
Or map files to the schema in the settings (.vscode/settings.json), with no change to the files:

{
  "json.schemas": [
    {
      "fileMatch": ["wmtk/*.json"],
      "url": "https://wildmeshing.github.io/wildmeshing-toolkit/schemas/wmtk_app.json"
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: From the specs
docs.text: The schemas are generated by docs/tools/gen_reference.py from the same *_spec.json files that the components validate their options against; python docs/tools/gen_reference.py --out DIR writes them locally. They mirror the specs' rules: types, defaults, allowed values, bounds, and which options are required. The components remain the authority: a file the schema accepts can still be refused for a combination of options the spec cannot express.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The wildmeshing package: the compiled bindings (wildmeshing._core, built from python/src) and a pure-Python part (python/wildmeshing). Every function and class has a docstring: help(wildmeshing.tetwild) lists the component's options. Installation explains how to build it.

import wildmeshing as wm

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
One function per component, with two calls:

wm.<component>(options) On files, as wmtk_app runs the same options. Returns None. wm.<component>(options, meshes) -> (outputs, report) In memory. meshes maps names to mesh dictionaries, and the options name their inputs; outputs maps names to mesh dictionaries (outputs["mesh"] is the result) and report is a dictionary. Nothing is written. Function Tutorial Reference wm.shortest_edge_collapse tutorial options wm.qslim tutorial options wm.isotropic_remeshing tutorial options wm.tetwild tutorial options wm.triwild tutorial options wm.simwild tutorial options wm.topological_offset tutorial options wm.manifold_extraction tutorial options wm.tracking tutorial options wm.prismatic_mesh work in progress options wm.c1_simplification work in progress options wm.wildmeshing(options[, meshes]) The same, with the component named by options["application"], as in a wmtk_app file. wm.components() -> list[str] The components' names. wm.spec(name) -> list[dict] A component's spec: the rules of its options (pointer, type, default, doc, ...), from which its reference is generated.

An option a component does not have logs a warning, and has no effect (except in topological_offset, which refuses it).

docs.title: Meshes and files
docs.text:
Mesh dictionaries are described in Calling components.

wm.read_mesh(path) -> dict Reads .msh (Gmsh 4.1), .obj, and libigl's surface formats (.stl, .off, .ply, ...). wm.write_mesh(path, mesh) Writes .msh or .vtu. wm.save(outputs, stem), wm.load(stem) -> dict A checkpoint of a memory result: <stem>.msh, and <stem>_envelope.msh when the result has an envelope. load returns exactly the arrays save wrote, in the same order, so a pipeline resumed from a checkpoint continues as it would have without one. wm.read_history(path) -> bytes, wm.write_history(path, history) A history file (history_output, volume_history_output) as the bytes a memory call returns in its report, and back.

docs.title: Maps
docs.text:
Built from the history an application recorded; see the tracking tutorial.

wm.Tracking(history), wm.Tracking.load(path) The map between a surface application's input and its output. to_output(ids, bary) and to_input(ids, bary) map points given as faces (int64, (n,)) and barycentric coordinates (float64, (n, 3)), and return them on the other side, -1 for a point with no image. input_faces, input_triangles and output_triangles name the faces of each side; build_warnings counts where the map is not a bijection. wm.CurveTracking(history), wm.CurveTracking.load(path) The same for curves (TriWild): points on segments, with feature_points. wm.VolumeTracking(...), wm.VolumeTracking.load(...) The map of a tet mesh's volume, region by region, from the surface and volume histories that TetWild and SimWild record with volume_history_output.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text: wm.Expression(expr, known_names) A parsed tag expression (names, &, |, !, parentheses, _; see Concepts: regions). eval(tags) evaluates it on a set of tag names; has_unknown_names() is true when it names a tag outside known_names.

docs.title: PolyFEM operations
docs.text: wildmeshing.polyfem_ops runs PolyFEM-based operations on .msh files (install with pip install ".[polyfem]", and set POLYFEM_BIN): see python/README.md.

docs.title: simwild: behaviours adopted from tetwild / triwild
docs.text:
tetwild and triwild are the mature, heavily-measured applications; simwild is a fork of them that drifted. When de-duplicating, the rule is: wherever the copies disagree, the tetwild/triwild implementation wins, and tetwild/triwild output must not move. simwild output may move, and every time it does the reason is recorded here so the simwild side can be re-checked later.

Columns: what simwild did, what it does now, which copy won, and what actually moved.

docs.title: 1a. SimWildMeshTri::swap_all_edges returns the success count
docs.text: was return true; — i.e. always 1, whatever happened now returns total_success from run_localized_to_convergence, and the pass uses parallel_collect_edge_ops + localized retry source triwild EdgeSwapping.cpp::swap_all_edges, which carries the fix and the note why it matters local_operations stops the swap loop when a pass changes nothing (if (cnt_success == 0) break;). Returning a constant 1 made that early exit unreachable. measured No output change on any of the 8 simwild 2D configs. The loop is bounded by ops[2], which is 1 in every current config, so there was never a second round for the early exit to skip. The defect is real but latent — like the split fallback in #1000, it needs a config that asks for more than one swap round per iteration. also adopted parallel_collect_edge_ops and run_localized_to_convergence, which simwild-2D used nowhere. Output-neutral here because the pass converges in one round on these inputs.

docs.title: 1b. SimWildMeshTri reports why smoothing was refused
docs.text: was m_smooth_rejects declared and passed to smooth_vertex_2d, but never reset() and never logged now reset at the top of each smoothing pass, to_string() logged at the end, as triwild does source triwild Smooth.cpp::smooth_all_vertices why it matters The counters exist precisely to catch silent failure — SmoothVertex.hpp:222-228 records tetwild smoothing ZERO vertices for entire runs without anything noticing. Accumulating them across passes and never printing them defeats that. measured No output change; diagnostics only.

docs.title: 1c. simwild-3D skips the Voronoi search for an un-rounded vertex
docs.text: was if (m_voronoi_split_fn) now if (m_voronoi_split_fn && m_vertex_attribute[v_id].m_is_rounded) source the 2D twin, SimWildMeshTri::split_edge_after, which already carried the guard and the reasoning why it matters When the rounded midpoint inverts a tet, the split falls back to the exact rational midpoint. The Voronoi bisection then searches only doubles — including the plain double midpoint it reverts to on failure, which is the position that just inverted. Neither tetwild nor triwild has a Voronoi split, so this is simwild-internal: the 2D copy was right and the 3D one had not been updated. measured No output change: no current config sets m_voronoi_split_fn and reaches the fallback.

docs.title: 1d. SimWildMesh::swap_edge_56_before stores the max energy it computes
docs.text: was computed max_energy over the incident tets and dropped it, leaving cache.max_energy holding whatever the previous swap op wrote now swap_cache.local().max_energy = max_energy; source tetwild EdgeSwapping.cpp:756 why it matters swap_cache is one thread-local shared by the 3-2 / 4-4 / 5-6 ops. Harmless only as long as swap_edge_56_after never reads it — but the sibling swap_edge_44_after and swap_edge_after both do. measured No output change.

docs.title: 1f. simwild-3D routes swap surface detection on the incident-face count
docs.text: was is_edge_on_surface(t), which short-circuits on both endpoints' m_is_on_surface flags now edge_incident_surface_face_count(t) > 0, ported from tetwild; applied at all three swap sites (3-2, 4-4, 5-6) source tetwild EdgeSwapping.cpp:144-151 and its comment why it matters A stale m_is_on_surface flag makes a genuine surface edge look interior, and swapping it tears the surface. The face-count route consults only the face attributes. measured No output change on the 6 simwild 3D configs — the flags are not stale on these inputs. not changed here simwild still rejects surface edges in 4-4 and 5-6 where tetwild allows a surface flip via its generalized prepare_surface_flip. That is a larger decision, deferred to the 3D base-class merge.

docs.title: 1e. The collapse quality gate — NO CHANGE, the premise was wrong
docs.text:
The duplication survey reported "four mutually incompatible spellings" of the quality gate in collapse_edge_before:

tetwild     VA[v1_id].m_is_rounded && q > cache.max_energy
simwild-3D  m_collapse_check_quality && VA[v1_id].m_is_rounded && q > cache.max_energy
triwild     VA[v1_id].m_is_rounded && q > m_params.stop_energy && q > cache.max_energy
simwild-2D  VA[v1_id].m_is_rounded && q > target_quality(tid)  && q > cache.max_energy

Checked before changing anything, and they are two rules, not four — one per dimension, each correctly adapted in simwild:

  • SimWildMeshTri::target_quality(tid) defaults to m_params.stop_energy and is only overridden by the per-tag quality_field. So simwild-2D's gate is triwild's, generalized to per-region targets. Replacing it with stop_energy would delete a simwild feature, not fix a divergence.
  • m_collapse_check_quality is an extra simwild-only toggle (switched off around simplify()), not a changed rule. simwild-3D's gate is otherwise tetwild's exactly.

The real open question is tetwild vs triwild. tetwild never permits a collapse that worsens the ring's worst element; triwild permits it as long as the result is still below the target. They disagree with each other, so "take the tetwild/triwild implementation" cannot resolve it. Left alone pending a decision and a measurement. See also 1i, the other tetwild/triwild disagreement.

docs.title: 1g. simwild-2D uses the shared utils::SizingField helpers
docs.text:
was refine_sizing_around_worst and gradation_smooth_sizing hand-rolled the top-N selection, the BFS region growth, the refinement clamp and the Dijkstra min-relaxation — ~100 lines re-implementing src/wmtk/utils/SizingField.hpp, which the other three meshes call now utils::select_worst_cells, grow_vertex_region, apply_sizing_refinement, gradation_smooth_sizing; 92 lines deleted source simwild-3D's refine_sizing_around_worst, which already had this shape measured No output change on any config.

Semantics deliberately preserved, not "corrected" to triwild's. triwild filters worst cells on an absolute filter_energy = min(max(max_energy/100, stop_energy), 100.); simwild filters on relative quality against the per-cell target_quality(tid) at a threshold of 1.0. That is simwild's model — its whole stop condition is per-cell relative quality — and simwild-3D already expresses it that way through the same shared helper. The hand-rolled 2D filter (if (q < target_quality(tid)) continue;) is exactly equivalent to it.

Still missing in simwild-2D, not addressed here (a feature port, not de-duplication): force-split of the worst cells' longest edges (m_force_split_edges), which tetwild, triwild and simwild-3D all have. skip_good_regions / active_vertices were adopted with the shared 2D smoothing pass in Stage 5 below.

docs.title: Decisions taken, not applied
docs.text: Two divergences turned out to be tetwild vs triwild, where "take the tetwild/triwild implementation" has no answer because the two reference apps disagree with each other.

docs.title: The collapse quality gate (see 1e) — deferred, decide with measurement
docs.text: tetwild and simwild-3D never permit a collapse that worsens the ring's worst element; triwild and simwild-2D permit it while the result stays below the target. Each fork already matches its own sibling, so nothing is inconsistent within a pair. Answering which rule is better is an optimizer-behaviour question needing a sweep of both variants on the challenging set, not a de-duplication question. Left as is. The 3D/2D base-class merge should surface it as one named virtual (e.g. collapse_allows_worsening_below_target()) so the choice is explicit in one place instead of implicit in four.

docs.title: tetwild's stale m_posf after the exact-midpoint split — separate PR
docs.text:
triwild, simwild-3D and simwild-2D all set p = to_double(m_pos) after falling back to the exact rational midpoint; tetwild alone keeps the average of the two endpoint doubles. triwild documents why its version is better: when an endpoint is itself un-rounded, rounding the exact midpoint once beats averaging two approximations.

Fixing tetwild necessarily moves tetwild output, which is the signal every de-duplication stage is validated against. Deferred to its own PR after the refactor, where a real output change is the expected result rather than a warning sign.

docs.title: Stage 1h — Parameters struct defaults now match their own spec defaults
docs.text:
Fourteen fields had a C++ struct default that disagreed with the JSON spec default for the same key, so any code path that builds Parameters without going through jse — which is what the unit tests do — ran a different configuration than every driver run:

app field struct was spec (now both) tetwild eps_rel 2e-3 1e-3 tetwild stop_energy 10 100 tetwild interleaved_smoothing false true tetwild interleaved_smoothing_passes 2 1 tetwild stuck_refine_num_worst 50 0 tetwild stuck_refine_rings 3 0 tetwild skip_good_regions true false triwild stop_energy 20 100 simwild skip_simplify true false simwild eps_simplify_rel 2e-3 2e-4 (10x) simwild preserve_topology false true simwild stuck_refine_num_worst 50 0 simwild stuck_refine_rings 3 0 simwild skip_good_regions true false

The spec is authoritative: it is what every driver run injects. No integration output moved, which is the expected result — the configs all go through jse. ctest 107/107, so the unit tests that construct Parameters directly either set these explicitly or are insensitive to them.

docs.title: report["#t"] counted faces, not tets, in simwild 3D
docs.text:
was report["#t"] = mesh.get_faces().size(); in run_3D — on a TetMesh that is the number of faces now mesh.get_tets().size() source tetwild reports tet_size(), triwild reports tri_capacity(); both mean cells measured The 6 simwild 3D configs report #t roughly halved — e.g. simwild_double_sphere_3d 22456 -> 10897, a ratio of 2.06, which is what a closed tet mesh gives since each interior face is shared by two tets. The mesh is unchanged; only the reported number was wrong.

run_2D was already correct: on a TriMesh the faces are the cells.

Note for future baselines: simwild 3D #t values recorded before this change are face counts.

docs.title: Stage 3a — simwild-2D adopts wmtk::TriOptimizerMesh
docs.text:
SimWildMeshTri now derives from the shared 2D base rather than from wmtk::TriMesh, and its copies of the three attribute types, the shared members and 13 methods are deleted in favour of the base's.

No simwild output moved, and no behaviour was adopted. This is the rare case where the policy ("when the two disagree, tetwild/triwild wins") had nothing to decide, because the two copies did not disagree anywhere. Every difference between simwild-2D's implementation and triwild's was cosmetic, and each was checked individually before the copy was deleted:

function the only difference is_inverted(array) const auto res vs auto res; return !(res > 0) vs an if/else; triwild carries a stale comment about orient3d that simwild had dropped (dropped here too) is_inverted(Tuple), is_inverted(size_t) simwild inlines the oriented_tri_vids temporary get_quality(Tuple), get_quality(size_t) same inlining get_quality(array) none — identical is_inverted_f simwild has only the size_t overload; the bodies match. It now also inherits the Tuple one round m_pos << posf[0], posf[1] vs to_rational(m_posf), which are the same value; both set m_is_rounded before the one-ring check. simwild's comment explaining why was the better one and was kept get_length2 get_edge_vids vs switch_vertex, same two vertices partition_mesh auto i vs size_t i as the loop variable (simwild's compares signed to unsigned) round_all_vertices, get_max_avg_energy, gradation_smooth_sizing, get_edges_by_condition, is_edge_on_surface x2, is_edge_on_bbox x2, vertex_is_on_surface, edge_is_on_surface none — identical after normalisation

The attribute types matched too: CellTag is a std::set<int64_t>, so FaceAttributes was already character-identical, and VertexAttributes differed only by triwild's m_feature_id, which simwild-2D leaves at NO_FEATURE.

Measured: all 53 registered configs byte-identical against the run immediately after the move commit — every simwild config included — plus ctest 107/107. tetwild_crown and tetwild_octocat run 10 threads and are nondeterministic there, so they were compared separately at num_threads: 0 against a build of the pre-refactor commit: byte-identical.

One thing to watch later: SimWildMeshTri keeps its own round_and_check_all_rounded, m_exact_split_count and triangle_area, none of which triwild has. The first two are the subject of Stage 4's RationalPositions mixin.

docs.title: Stage 3b — simwild-3D adopts wmtk::TetOptimizerMesh
docs.text:
SimWildMesh now derives from the shared 3D base, dropping its copies of VertexAttributes, FaceAttributes, the vertex and face attribute collections, the envelope/solver/rounding members, MAX_ENERGY, and 23 method definitions.

Of the 21 methods the base owns, 19 were already byte-identical between the two applications and two (get_quality, output_faces) differed only cosmetically -- auto vs bool for a local, and an (int) cast on a row assignment into a matrix that is already int. That leaves exactly one behavioural adoption:

docs.title: round() now marks the vertex rounded before the one-ring check
docs.text:
was simwild left m_is_rounded false until every incident tet had been checked, so is_inverted took the exact rational branch throughout the check now tetwild's: m_is_rounded is set before the loop and cleared again on failure, so is_inverted takes the float branch source tetwild, triwild and simwild-2D all already did it this way; simwild-3D was the only one that did not

This is answer-preserving, not merely close. The check asks whether the ROUNDED position keeps every incident tet valid. Under the old order the vertex's m_pos had already been set to to_rational(m_posf) -- exactly the double, as a rational -- so the rational branch evaluated the orientation of the same four points that the float branch evaluates with orient3d, which is itself exact for the doubles it is handed. Both branches also fall back to rational identically when some other incident vertex is un-rounded, since is_inverted tests all four flags. The difference is cost, not result: simwild was paying for exact arithmetic to compute an answer the float predicate already decides exactly.

docs.title: Not adopted in this commit
docs.text:
The swap family stays per-application and is untouched here: swap_face_before, swap_face_after, swap_edge_after and swap_all_faces all propagate simwild's CellTag through the operation, which tetwild has no counterpart for. Sharing them needs a tag-propagation hook. Three differences found while measuring them are recorded here so they are not lost:

  • swap_all_faces collects the wrong simplex. simwild calls parallel_collect_edge_ops and queues "face_swap" operations on edge tuples -- 6 per tet -- where tetwild calls parallel_collect_face_ops and queues them on faces, 4 per tet. The face-swap pass therefore enumerates a different set, with each face reachable from up to three of its edges.
  • simwild calls the executor directly where tetwild uses run_localized_to_convergence.
  • simwild reads the success count from executor.get_cnt_success() after the lambda has returned; tetwild accumulates it into a captured local.

At this stage smoothing_energy_envelope stayed per-application. Stage 6 below subsequently removed SimWild's redundant surface-envelope alias and adopted TetWild's order->= 2 selection; only the application-specific order-2 envelope object remains virtual.

smooth_after stays in both applications even though their bodies are byte-identical: the body is the shared optimization::smooth_vertex_3d template, which reaches m_tet_attribute and smoothing_energy_envelope, both per-application.

docs.title: Stage 3c — simwild adopts wmtk::run_pass
docs.text:
The if (NUM_THREADS > 0) / build an ExecutePass / install a lock / log the time shell around every driver is now wmtk::run_pass, shared by all four meshes. No simwild behaviour changed: the shell was already identical to tetwild's and triwild's in all eleven simwild drivers, and what each driver does inside the executor is passed in as a callback, so the differences below survive the fold untouched rather than being silently adopted.

They are listed here because folding the shell is what makes them visible, and because each one is now a one-line change instead of a rewrite:

simwild tetwild / triwild how the pass runs executor(mesh, ops) once, in 3D split, all four 3D swaps and 2D split/smooth run_localized_to_convergence(mesh, executor, ops) — retries a failure only where the mesh actually changed that round 2D collapse a hand-rolled do { ... } while (executor.get_cnt_success() > 0) that rebuilds the whole op list from get_edges() every round the same localized retry as everything else success count executor.get_cnt_success(), i.e. the last round's count the total accumulated across rounds by the retry driver

The success-count row matters where the caller uses the return value to decide whether to keep going: local_operations stops its swap loop once a pass changes nothing, and a per-round count and a total disagree about when that is. simwild-2D's swap already takes the shared form (Stage 1a); the 3D swaps do not.

Adopting the localized form is a real behaviour change for simwild -- it changes which failed operations are re-tested and in what order -- so it wants its own commit and its own before/after, not a line in a refactor.

docs.title: Post-3c — simwild adopts the localized retry and the accumulated success count
docs.text:
Closes the three differences Stage 3c recorded but deliberately left alone. Every driver now runs its pass the way its sibling does.

driver was now 3D split, all five 3D swaps, 2D split executor(mesh, ops) — a single pass, so an operation rejected early was dropped even when a later success next to it made it viable run_localized_to_convergence, which re-runs until a pass yields nothing, re-queueing only failures adjacent to a vertex that moved that round 2D collapse do { all_ops.clear(); for (e : get_edges()) …; executor(…); } while (get_cnt_success() > 0) — converged, but by re-enumerating every edge and re-running the full geometric pre-check on each one, every round the same shared retry driver, off an op list built once the five 3D swaps' return value executor.get_cnt_success(), the last round's count the total accumulated across rounds

The return value is not bookkeeping: local_operations stops its swap loop when a pass reports zero, and a pass that has converged ends on a zero round by construction, so the old form made the loop stop after one round of swaps regardless of how much work remained.

The 2D collapse needed a renew_neighbor_tuples — its rebuild-everything loop never had one, and the retry driver takes the modified region from exactly that callback. It is triwild's.

Not adopted here, still open: simwild builds its op lists with a serial for (const Tuple& e : get_edges()) where tetwild and triwild use parallel_collect_edge_ops. That changes the queue's insertion order, which breaks ties in the priority queue, so it is its own behaviour change and would have blurred this one's before/after.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
Four configs moved; every triwild and deterministic tetwild config is byte-identical, and the branch touches no file outside components/simwild/.

config before after simwild_curves_2d 572 tris, avg 2.385, max 8.294 384 tris, avg 2.499, max 8.494 simwild_curves_two_inputs_2d 465 tris, avg 3.343, max 18.862 871 tris, avg 2.815, max 18.844 simwild_remeshing_2d 211 tris, avg 2.299, max 4.330 246 tris, avg 2.324, max 4.188 simwild_double_sphere_notop_3d 21454 tets, avg 3.6171 21459 tets, avg 3.6170

The direction is mixed, and the mechanism is visible in simwild_curves_2d's log. The split pass now converges instead of running once, so the mesh refines far harder mid-run -- 1955 edges at iteration 5 where it used to reach 695 -- and the collapse pass then pulls it back further than before, to 378. The optimizer takes a different trajectory rather than a uniformly finer or coarser one. Collapse itself is unchanged in aggregate: the first call's rounds used to sum to ~316 successes and the shared driver now reports 313.

docs.title: Post-3c — simwild adopts parallel_collect_edge_ops
docs.text:
The last collection-side difference. simwild built three op lists with a serial for (const Tuple& e : get_edges()) -- 3D split, 2D split, 2D collapse -- where tetwild and triwild use the shared parallel builder. Held back from the localized-retry change because it alters the queue's insertion order, which is what breaks ties between equal-priority operations, and mixing the two would have made neither before/after attributable.

Measured: nothing moved. All 53 registered configs are byte-identical, simwild's four included -- the same four that moved for the retry adoption. The tie-breaking concern is real in principle and did not materialize on any config in the suite.

That leaves simwild's op collection identical to its sibling's everywhere except swap_all_faces, which is still parallel_collect_edge_ops where tetwild uses parallel_collect_face_ops -- that one is a defect rather than a style difference (6 edge tuples per tet instead of 4 faces) and is recorded above with the rest of the swap family.

docs.title: Post-3c — swap_all_faces collects faces
docs.text:
The defect recorded with the swap family, fixed on its own because it is a behaviour change rather than a sharing question.

SimWildMesh::swap_all_faces called parallel_collect_edge_ops and queued "face_swap" operations on edge tuples -- 6 per tet, with each face reachable from up to three of its edges -- where tetwild calls parallel_collect_face_ops and queues them on faces, 4 per tet. The pass therefore enumerated a different set of simplices from the one it is named for, seeding the priority queue with duplicates of some faces and a different traversal for the rest.

Two configs move, both of them the 3D ones that actually run face swaps:

config before after simwild_double_sphere_3d — same #t/#v, different connectivity simwild_double_sphere_notop_3d 21459 tets, avg 3.616959 21528 tets, avg 3.617020

Everything else in the suite is byte-identical, and the branch touches no file outside components/simwild/.

Both remaining swap differences are settled below.

docs.title: Post-3c — simwild adopts tetwild's swap family, with tag propagation
docs.text: The last item in the de-duplication programme, and the largest single behaviour change in it. components/simwild/.../EdgeSwapping.cpp is now tetwild's file: after renaming the mesh class and the parameters struct, the only lines that differ are the tag handling described below and one swap_all_faces comment. Every remaining divergence has been resolved in tetwild's favour.

docs.title: Why tags and the surface are the same question
docs.text:
simwild's surface is not an input mesh — init_surfaces_and_boundaries tags a face m_is_surface_fs exactly when its two tets carry different tags. So a surface diagonal flip in simwild is a flip of the tag interface, and the volume it sweeps (the tet (a,b,c,d) between the old and new diagonal) moves from one tag to the other. That is the same thing tetwild's flip does across its inside/outside surface, and it is gated the same way, by the Hausdorff envelope check on the two new faces.

Two consequences fall out and are used throughout:

  • An edge with no incident surface face has all its incident tets identically tagged, so an interior swap has nothing to decide.
  • The two surface faces (a,b,c), (a,b,d) cut the ring of incident tets into two arcs, one tag each — and every tet a flip creates contains at least one ring vertex other than c,d, which says which arc, hence which tag, it belongs to.

docs.title: What simwild adopted
docs.text:
before after prepare_surface_flip prepare_surface_flip_32: exactly-3 ring only, log_and_throw_error on anything unexpected, asserts that (c,d) already exists tetwild's, generalized to any ring size; rejects rather than throws; handles (c,d) not existing yet, which is the normal case for 4-4 and 5-6 4-4 and 5-6 on a surface edge rejected outright (edge_incident_surface_face_count > 0 → false) steered to the case that realizes the flip, by swap_edge_44_accept_case / swap_edge_56_accept_case, then envelope-checked and re-tagged like the 3→2 case the (c,d) non-manifold guard assert + get_surface_faces_for_edge tetwild's direct enumeration, which does not depend on the possibly-stale m_is_on_surface vertex flags the "would-be new faces already surface" guard absent tetwild's, gated on lowest_common_tet so a Debug build does not abort on every 4-4 flip swap_edge_56_after re-checked is_inverted tetwild's: swap_edge_56_energy returns double::max() for any inverted candidate and the case is only taken when strictly below the old energy, so the check could never fire swap_all_edges_44 / _56 no check_surface_topology guard tetwild's guard, now that these can change the surface swap_all_edges_all logged its topology warning as "swap_all_edges_32" its own name counters cnt_surface_swap only plus tetwild's cnt_surface_swap_32/44/56 breakdown, and the same log line open-boundary edges not considered wmtk::TetOptimizerMesh::is_open_boundary_edge, a new virtual that defaults to false and that tetwild overrides — see below

is_open_boundary_edge defaulting to false is exact for simwild, not a stub: around an interior edge the tags change an even number of times going around the tet ring, so the interface can never terminate there; it can only end where it meets the bbox, and is_edge_on_bbox has already rejected those edges by the time the question is asked. Making it a virtual is what leaves the two prepare_surface_flip bodies byte-identical.

docs.title: The tag rule
docs.text:
Three simwild-only additions, and nothing else:

  • cache_interior_swap_tag — no incident surface face, so record the one tag the incident tets share. If they disagree the swap is refused: that can only happen if the tag/surface invariant is already broken elsewhere, and re-tagging would move tagged volume with no envelope check to gate it. This replaces the old 3→2 rule (majority vote over at most two tags) and the old 4-4 / 5-6 rule (take incident_tets[0], with a commented-out check that they all agree).
  • prepare_surface_flip additionally records ring_tags: for each ring vertex other than c,d, the tag of its side.
  • propagate_swap_tags — interior swap: give every new tet the cached tag. Surface flip: give each new tet the tag of the arc its ring vertices identify, and refuse if a tet straddles both arcs or touches neither.

On a well-formed mesh this leaves the 3→2 result unchanged: an interior edge has one tag, so the majority vote agreed with it, and on a surface edge the majority is by construction the arc holding two of the three tets, which is the arc both new tets land in.

SwapInfoCache::sf_e is gone — the third apex of the 3→2 ring, which nothing read.

docs.title: Measured
docs.text:
tetwild and triwild are byte-identical, on all 53 registered configs — with tetwild_crown and tetwild_octocat re-run at num_threads: 0, since at their configured 10 they are nondeterministic by construction — and on all 30 hidden [challenging] models (14 tetwild Thingi10K, 16 triwild20k), compared against two independent baselines: the run for #1011 and the run for #1009, which also agree with each other. The comparison is every report.json field except the timing keys, plus the md5 of every emitted mesh — out_final.msh, out_simplified_input.obj, out_surface.obj for tetwild and out.msh, out.vtu, out_surf.vtu for triwild.

Two simwild configs move, the only two that run 3D swaps:

config before after simwild_double_sphere_3d 10897 tets, 2198 verts, avg 3.80078 10888 tets, 2197 verts, avg 3.79623 simwild_double_sphere_notop_3d 21528 tets, 4257 verts, avg 3.61702, max 8.5319 21311 tets, 4215 verts, avg 3.59206, max 8.7158

Both get slightly smaller at slightly better average energy, and the counters say exactly why:

config surface flips before surface flips after simwild_double_sphere_3d 4 85 = 4 (3→2) + 69 (4-4) + 12 (5-6) simwild_double_sphere_notop_3d 0 89 = 1 (3→2) + 70 (4-4) + 18 (5-6)

The 3→2 count on the first config is unchanged, which is the claim above about the tag rule being behaviour-preserving there, measured rather than argued. All of the movement is the 4-4 and 5-6 flips that simwild used to refuse outright — the ones that let the optimizer relieve a bad configuration on the interface instead of routing around it. (notop's 3→2 going 0 → 1 is downstream: the mesh reaches configurations it never used to.)

Re-running both with check_surface_topology: true — which takes a full topological signature of the tracked surface (V, E, F, Euler, components, boundary loops) before each swap pass and reports any change afterwards — gives zero complaints across all 174 flips. A diagonal flip is supposed to leave surface topology alone, and on real data it does.

docs.title: Tested
docs.text:
test_simwild_swap_tags.cpp builds an N-tet ring whose two arcs carry different tags, derives the surface from the tags the way init_surfaces_and_boundaries does, runs the flip, and checks that every face is surface iff its two tets still disagree — for the 3→2, 4-4 and 5-6 flips, plus an interior swap that must preserve its single tag. The 4-4 and 5-6 cases assert the resulting tets by vid, so a wrong side would fail rather than merely a wrong count. Release and Debug.

Writing it turned up an unrelated latent defect in simwild's test-only create_mesh_attributes, fixed here: it assigned m_tet_attribute.m_attributes a vector sized to the live tet count, shrinking the collection below the connectivity capacity that init() had reserved. An AttributeCollection deliberately never grows during an operation, so a 5→6 swap indexed one past the end. tetwild carried the same bug and had already fixed it (ASan found it there); this is the same fix, and simwild's version segfaults outright rather than corrupting quietly because the field being written is a std::set and not a double.

docs.title: 2D was already done
docs.text:
For completeness, since "adopt all the swaps" covers both dimensions: the 2D swap family (swap_all_edges, swap_weight, swap_edge_before, swap_edge_after) is already identical between triwild and simwild-2D — after renaming the mesh class, the only differences are two comments. Stage 3a's shared TriOptimizerMesh::FaceAttributes carries tags for both, so even the tag lines are common code, and SwapInfoCache::face_tags is triwild's too. (triwild has carried an unused std::set<int64_t> tags per triangle since well before this programme — see git show origin/main:.../TriWildMesh.h — so that is pre-existing, not something the move added.)

The tag propagation is correct there for a simpler reason than in 3D: the 2D swap opens with if (is_edge_on_surface(t)) return false;, and in 2D too the surface is the tag interface (SimWildMeshTri::init_surfaces_and_boundaries), so a 2D swap only ever runs on an edge whose two faces already agree. cache.face_tags = FA[incident_faces[0]].tags is then exact. There is no 2D counterpart to the 4-4 / 5-6 question because a 2-2 flip is the only edge swap a triangle mesh has.

docs.title: Stage 4 — one swap engine, with serial Wild/Sim conformance tests
docs.text:
The identical implementations described above are no longer merely kept in sync:

  • TriWild's complete 2D swap pass now lives on TriOptimizerMesh. Both TriWildMesh and SimWildMeshTri inherit the same collector, priority calculation, retry/termination logic, before/after callbacks, quality gate, attribute tracker and face-tag propagation.
  • TetWild's complete 3D swap family now lives on TetOptimizerMesh: 3→2, 4→4, 5→6, 2→3 face swaps, the combined pass, surface-diagonal handling and topology diagnostics. SimWild's old 858-line copy is a small adapter implementing only three tag hooks: cache one homogeneous interior tag, cache the two surface-ring arcs, and propagate those tags to new cells.
  • TetWild's 3D smoothing pass and acceptance callback also live on TetOptimizerMesh. The only application policy left virtual is which envelope supplies the surface energy/containment check. Quality reads and writes go through the common cell-quality accessors, so TetWild's pass ordering and rejection rules are used unchanged with SimWild's tagged cell attributes.

test_wild_conformance.cpp enforces the intended oracle relationship directly. It constructs two identical meshes, runs the Wild implementation first and tag-homogeneous SimWild second with NUM_THREADS == 0, then compares operation counts, canonical connectivity, per-cell quality and vertex positions; the SimWild side must additionally preserve its homogeneous tag. There is one fixture for TriWild/SimWild 2D and one for TetWild/SimWild 3→2. These are deliberately serial: a parallel A/B test can turn shared global state or nondeterministic scheduling into noise and does not establish that SimWild followed the Wild path. A third fixture runs the shared TetWild/SimWild 3D smoothing pass serially and compares the same geometry, exact positions and qualities while checking that SimWild's cell tags are untouched.

Two audit fixes were made alongside the extraction:

  • stop_at_float now applies to SimWild 2D as well as 3D.
  • the public 3D replace_tags rejects mismatched input/output vector lengths, matching its 2D counterpart instead of indexing past found_tags.

docs.title: Stage 5 — one 2D smoothing pass
docs.text:
TriWild's complete smoothing pass now lives on TriOptimizerMesh, matching the already-shared 3D pass on TetOptimizerMesh. Both TriWildMesh and SimWildMeshTri inherit the same vertex collection/order, rounding and bbox gate, two-stage solve, inversion/envelope/quality rejection, quality updates, rejection counters, and skip_good_regions selection. The shared base also owns the identical floating/exact position reads and writes.

Both applications use the base's single m_envelope for the pull energy and containment. Its geometry is application-specific -- TriWild builds it around its input curves, while SimWild can build it around the interface between different cell tags -- but there is only one envelope per 2D mesh. The only smoothing acceptance policy left virtual is the positional constraint: TriWild uses it to preserve feature points and SimWild, which has no separate 0-dimensional features, always accepts it.

Two SimWild behaviors deliberately move to TriWild's ground truth:

  • SimWild no longer sets quality_veto_on_surface = false; a surface move that worsens the worst incident triangle is rejected in both applications.
  • SimWild now honors skip_good_regions; a vertex incident only to triangles below skip_good_regions_margin * stop_energy is not scheduled for smoothing.
  • SimWild's unused 2D m_envelope_orig alias is deleted. Energy and containment both use m_envelope, exactly as in TriWild. This does not change the standard remeshing path because the two pointers aliased the same object there.

The serial conformance fixture runs TriWild first and tag-homogeneous SimWild second from identical 2D meshes, then compares connectivity, floating and exact positions, per-face qualities, and tags. It separately enables skip_good_regions, makes every face good, and verifies both applications schedule zero vertices. Full TriWild and SimWild test suites pass.

docs.title: Stage 6 — envelope and refinement parity
docs.text:
SimWild 3D now has the same envelope model as TetWild: one surface m_envelope, plus the separate order-2 feature envelope. The old m_envelope_orig pointer was always assigned from m_envelope and is deleted. Feature pulling now uses TetWild's exact condition, order >= 2, including order-3 junction vertices, and falls back to the surface envelope when no initialized feature envelope exists.

The remaining refinement gaps are also closed:

  • SimWild 2D records the longest edge of each selected worst triangle in m_force_split_edges, matching TriWild.
  • SimWild 3D applies TetWild's oversized-only force-split guard, including the JSON option.
  • active_vertices() is virtual at the optimizer bases. Wild keeps its absolute global threshold; SimWild overrides it by normalizing every cell against its tag-dependent target_quality().

The serial conformance suite now also covers 3D 4→4, 5→6, 2→3, and combined swaps; order-3 feature-envelope selection; 2D/3D force-split refinement; per-tag active-region filtering; and heterogeneous-tag split/collapse invariants in both dimensions.

docs.title: Stage 7 — shared outer optimization drivers
docs.text:
The outer schedules now live on the dimensional optimizer bases:

  • TetOptimizerMesh owns the complete TetWild/SimWild 3D driver and its local_operations pass.
  • TriOptimizerMesh owns the complete TriWild/SimWild-2D driver and its local_operations pass.
  • the smoothing placement parameters (num_smoothing_passes, interleaved_smoothing, and interleaved_smoothing_passes) live in OptimizerParameters, so all three components configure the same schedule.

TetWild and TriWild remain the behavioral sources of truth: pre- and post-collapse, interleaved or batched split/collapse/swap/smooth ordering, per-phase convergence checks, rounding, consolidation, stuck refinement, swap termination, debug output, and sanity checks are executed by their shared base. The application classes no longer contain copies of either driver.

Only explicit policy hooks differ. Wild uses absolute AMIPS and stop_energy; SimWild reports quality normalized by each cell's tag-dependent target and stops at relative quality 1. SimWild also supplies its existing optional stop_at_float policy and tag-aware refinement, while TetWild retains its extra open-boundary sanity diagnostic.

The conformance suite now runs one complete iteration under both the batched and interleaved schedules, serially from identical meshes in each dimension: TriWild then homogeneous SimWild-2D, and TetWild then homogeneous SimWild-3D. It compares iteration counts, canonical connectivity, per-cell qualities, floating and exact positions, and checks that SimWild kept its homogeneous tags and derived interface invariant.

docs.title: Tracking: recording, mapping, extending
docs.text: Notes on the tracking framework added for BijectiveRemesh (arXiv 2605.30744): how it works, how to use it, how to bring it to another application, and how to check that it is right, for surfaces and for curves (triwild). File paths are relative to the repository root; the memory interface is in docs/in-memory-io.md.

docs.title: What it is for
docs.text:
An application that remeshes a surface -- or a tet mesh whose tracked faces are a surface -- can record every change it makes to that surface. From the record (a history, saved as a tracking file) the tracking component rebuilds a map between the input surface and the output surface, both ways. Users map their own points, and through them their own attributes: labels, texture coordinates, any per-vertex or per-face data.

The map is built as BijectiveRemesh builds it: one local map per operation, between the patch the operation replaced and the patch it left, composed in order. Where every local map is a bijection, so is the whole map.

The same holds one dimension down. triwild tracks curves -- the input's segments, inserted as edges of its triangle mesh -- and records every change to them; the map then takes the input curves onto the output's tracked edges, and the input's feature points (curve ends, junctions, input points) onto the output vertices they became. See Curves below.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Turn tracking on with history_output -- the same option in every application that has it: isotropic_remeshing, qslim, shortest_edge_collapse, tetwild, simwild (surfaces) and triwild (curves).

{"application": "tetwild", "input": ["model.obj"], "output": "out", "history_output": "out.wmtkhist"}

On the memory route (name(options, meshes), see docs/in-memory-io.md) no file is written: any non-empty history_output records the history, and the report returns it as history, the bytes of the file the file route writes (bytes in Python). history::write_history / wm.write_history save them as that file. simwild also returns the mesh its history starts from as the output mesh history_input. tetwild and simwild can track the volume around the surface too, with volume_history_output: see Volumes.

Map points with the tracking application of the same wmtk_app binary:

{"application": "tracking", "history": "out.wmtkhist", "operation": "map",
 "points": "points.txt", "output_points": "mapped.txt", "direction": "to_output"}

points.txt holds one point per line; numbers separated by blanks; # starts a comment. - On the input: face b0 b1 b2. face is a triangle of the input files, counting from 0 over all of them in order, as the files hold them. b are barycentric coordinates with respect to that triangle's corners, in file order. - On the input of a history that starts at a tet mesh's tracked surface (simwild on a .msh): v0 v1 v2 b0 b1 b2, as on a tet output, with the v vertices of the tet mesh the history starts from (<output>_history_input.msh). - On the output of a surface application (isotropic_remeshing): face b0 b1 b2, with face a triangle of the output file. - On the output of a tet application (tetwild, simwild): v0 v1 v2 b0 b1 b2. The v are three vertices of the output tet mesh, at the corners of a tracked face. The tracked surface is no element of the tet mesh file, so the vertices name the face. They may come in any order; the coordinates follow them.

direction is to_output or to_input (the inverse map). A point with no image comes back with id -1.

On curves (triwild) the file says it holds curves, and the points are: - on the input: segment b0 b1. segment is a segment of the input curve files, counting from 0 over all of them in order -- a polyline l line gives its consecutive vertex pairs -- and b are barycentric coordinates with respect to its ends in file order; - on the output: v0 v1 b0 b1, two vertices of the output mesh at the ends of a tracked edge, in either order, the coordinates following them.

"operation": "features" writes the input's feature points to output_points, one input_vertex output_vertex per line: a vertex of the input files (the curve files' vertices in order, then the point files') and the output vertex it ended at, -1 for none; on the memory route it returns them in the report instead, as feature_points.

From C++ (components/tracking/wmtk/components/tracking/tracking.hpp, the component's one public header):

const auto t = tracking::Tracking::load("out.wmtkhist");
std::vector<tracking::InputPoint> pts = {{face, {b0, b1, b2}}};
auto on_output = t.to_output(pts);    // OutputPoint: .face, or .vertices for a tet output
auto back = t.to_input(on_output);    // InputPoint: .face, or .vertices (input_by_vertices)
auto triangles = t.output_triangles(); // the output's tracked faces, in its own ids

// Curves: the same, one dimension down.
const auto c = tracking::CurveTracking::load("curves.wmtkhist");
std::vector<tracking::InputCurvePoint> on_input = {{segment, {b0, b1}}};
auto on_curves = c.to_output(on_input);   // OutputCurvePoint: .vertices, two mesh vertices
auto features = c.feature_points();       // {input_vertex, output_vertex} per feature point

From Python, the same classes on NumPy arrays (python/src/tracking_bindings.cpp), built from the history's bytes -- a memory call's report["history"], or wm.read_history -- or from its file:

outputs, report = wm.isotropic_remeshing({"input": "in", "history_output": "x"}, {"in": mesh})
t = wm.Tracking(report["history"])          # smoothing="flatten", scaffold="box",
                                            # collapse_patch="both_stars"; or .load(path)
ids, bary = t.to_output(faces, bary)        # int64 (n,), float64 (n, 3) -> the output's
faces, bary = t.to_input(ids, bary)         # and back
ids, bary, warnings = t.to_output(faces, bary, warnings=True)  # what this call found

c = wm.CurveTracking(triwild_report["history"])   # or .load(path)
pairs, bary = c.to_output(segments, bary)   # int64 (n,), float64 (n, 2) -> (n, 2) vertex pairs
c.feature_points()                          # int64 (p, 2): input vertex, output vertex
  • Ids. A face (segment) per point, (n,), or a mesh's vertices, (n, 3) -- (n, 2) on curves -- on a side named by vertices (output_by_vertices, input_by_vertices): tetwild's and simwild's output, simwild's input from a tet mesh, triwild's output. -1 is no face, both ways; a point with no image comes back with -1 and NaN coordinates. Shapes and dtypes are checked: TypeError for a dtype that is not an integer (ids) or a float (bary), ValueError for a shape that is not the side's.
  • Warnings. warnings=True returns a third element, the dictionary of what that call found (the keys of info's to_input_warnings); build_warnings is the map's.
  • Properties. input_faces, input_triangles, output_triangles (surfaces), input_segments, output_segments (curves): owning int64 arrays, in the ids points use.
  • Threads. Building the map releases the GIL and holds the lock component calls hold, as it logs through their logger; mapping releases the GIL and writes nothing, so several threads may map through one object. A damaged history raises RuntimeError; a curve history given to Tracking (or the reverse), or a volume history to either, raises ValueError, naming the other class.

Worked examples, one per application, are unit tests: - components/tracking/wmtk/components/tracking/tests/test_tracking.cpp (isotropic) - components/tetwild/wmtk/components/tetwild/tests/test_tetwild_tracking.cpp - components/simwild/wmtk/components/simwild/tests/test_simwild_tracking.cpp - components/qslim/wmtk/components/qslim/tests/test_qslim_tracking.cpp - components/shortest_edge_collapse/wmtk/components/shortest_edge_collapse/tests/test_sec_tracking.cpp - components/triwild/wmtk/components/triwild/tests/test_triwild_tracking.cpp (curves)

Each one runs the application with tracking on, maps random input points to the output and back, remaps a per-vertex attribute onto the output's vertices, and does the same from the command line with a points file.

On the memory route the applications record the same history, from the meshes they are given as from their files, and return it as bytes, curves as surfaces. tracking(options, meshes) takes the history as bytes: it runs info on a surface or a curve history and returns its report, transfer on a surface, and features on curves, whose report holds the feature points (feature_points, pairs of an input and an output vertex, -1 for none), and volume on a volume history's bytes (see Volumes); map and map_volume, whose points are text files, throw there: Tracking, CurveTracking and VolumeTracking map points in memory. The tests tracking-memory-route (isotropic) and tracking-memory-route-triwild (curves) run both.

Remapping attributes: - Per face. Map each output face's centroid to_input and take the input face's value. The transfer operation does this. - Per vertex. Map each output vertex to_input as a corner of one of its faces (barycentric (1,0,0) and its permutations) and interpolate there. - Per corner, with discontinuities (texture coordinates and their seams). The transfer operation evaluates each corner just inside its face, so that a corner on a seam lands in its own chart. This needs the output to conform to the seams (see Features below).

docs.title: The history
docs.text:
src/wmtk/history/History.hpp. History<N> records a complex whose faces have N corners: SurfaceHistory (N = 3, triangles) or CurveHistory (N = 2, segments; the faces of a curve history are its segments). history/Fwd.hpp names them all: Replay/CurveReplay, Recorder/CurveRecorder, TrackedSurfaceRecorder/TrackedCurveRecorder are aliases of BasicReplay<N>, BasicRecorder<N>, TrackedRecorder<N>. A history holds: - A snapshot of the complex: vertex and face slots, live or not. - Features: cells one dimension down that the edits keep -- feature edges of a surface, feature points of curves. See Features below. - The edits, in commit order. - metadata: free text. The applications store their JSON parameters there, with route, file or memory (ComponentIO::history_metadata), which is how tracking finds an application's input files when it is not given them -- and knows that a history recorded on the memory route names meshes, not files, and refuses to look for them. - output_vertex_ids: for applications whose output numbers vertices its own way. - input_vertex_ids: the same for the first state, for a history that starts at a tet mesh's tracked surface rather than at input files: the mesh's id of each snapshot vertex (TrackedSurfaceRecorder fills it). Empty for a history from files.

Edits are described on the complex alone -- vertex and face ids, positions -- never on the mesh class that did them. A TriMesh and the tracked surface of a TetMesh record in the same terms.

docs.title: Edit kinds
docs.text:
kind ids meaning split_edge v = {v0, v1, new}; faces in pairs (f, new_f) each face on the edge keeps its v0 half (v1 renamed new in place); new_f is f with v0 renamed new split_face v = {v0, v1, v2, new}; faces {f, f1, f2} surfaces only. f, f1 and f2 are the three faces at the new vertex, each the old face with one corner renamed collapse_edge v = {removed, kept} faces with both go; removed is renamed kept elsewhere; duplicate faces merge into the smallest id; a vertex left without faces is retired swap_edge v = {v0, v1, a, b}; faces {fa, fb} surfaces only. Edge (v0,v1) becomes (a,b): in fa (apex b) v1 becomes a, in fb (apex a) v0 becomes b move_vertices none only positions change consolidate none live vertices and faces renumbered by rank replace_faces v = corners of added faces; faces = removed, then added a change no other kind describes; no correspondence; the map cannot follow it relabel v = new id per vertex slot; faces = new id per face slot, or empty for rank order vertices renamed in place (several may become one); faces with a repeated corner go; several faces given one id become one, with the first's corners. The weld, a coordinate change, a reordering. A point keeps its barycentric coordinates embed v = corners of the new complex; faces = per new face, its sources (count, then ids), then the features the complex is replaced by one lying on it (an insertion, an arrangement). A point keeps its place in space

On curves the rules read the same with segments for faces: a split's face on the edge is the segment itself, a collapse removes the segment it collapses and merges duplicates.

Every edit carries moves: the position, after the edit, of every live vertex it wrote. Positions that did not change are dropped.

Replay (src/wmtk/history/Replay.hpp) applies edits with exactly these semantics. After the k-th edit it holds the recording mesh's surface after its k-th committed operation: the same ids, corner order and positions. Everything downstream relies on that.

Composition (History.hpp): - history::append(h, next). next starts exactly where h ends. It checks live vertices and faces, then appends next's edits. - history::append_embedded(h, next, sources). next starts on a complex lying on h's last state. It appends an embed edit, then next's edits.

docs.title: File format
docs.text:
Binary, varints (History.cpp). Version 7 is the first released one; the earlier ones were development formats and no longer load. A byte after the version gives N, the corners of a face: 3 for a surface, 2 for curves. Faces carry N ids and features N - 1. history::face_size(path) (or face_size(bytes)) reads it, and loading a history as the other kind throws. When you add to the format, bump kVersion, keep loading version 7 and up, and note in the comment at the top of the file what each version added.
