docs.text:
• Tracking: recording, mapping, extending: the complete notes, including how to record a new application and how the map's correctness is measured.
  • The tracking tutorial.
  • In-memory I/O for histories on the memory route.

docs.title: Local operations
docs.text: Every algorithm in the toolkit changes a mesh through a small set of local operations: edge split, edge collapse, edge and face swaps, vertex smoothing. Each one rewrites the cells around a few vertices and leaves the rest of the mesh alone. This page describes the mesh they work on, how code points at an element of it, what each operation does, and what happens around an operation: the hooks an algorithm writes, the invariants it checks, and the rollback when one of them fails.

docs.title: A mesh is connectivity plus attributes
docs.text:
The toolkit has two mesh classes: wmtk::TriMesh, a triangle mesh (a surface in 3D, or a 2D domain), and wmtk::TetMesh, a tetrahedral mesh. They store connectivity only:

  • for each cell (triangle or tetrahedron), its vertices;
  • for each vertex, the sorted list of the cells incident to it.

Edges and faces are not stored; they are derived from these two lists when needed. A removed cell or vertex is flagged, not erased, so ids stay valid during a pass; consolidate_mesh() compacts the storage afterwards and renumbers everything.

Everything else is an attribute: positions, sizing, quality, tags. An algorithm defines plain structs for the data it needs on vertices, edges, faces and cells, stores them in wmtk::AttributeCollection<T>, and registers the collections with the mesh. The mesh classes know nothing about geometry; a position is an attribute like any other. Shortest edge collapse, for instance, keeps this per vertex (ShortestEdgeCollapse.h):

struct VertexAttributes
{
    Eigen::Vector3d pos;
    size_t partition_id = 0;
    bool freeze = false;
    bool input_boundary = false;
};

and registers it in its constructor (ShortestEdgeCollapse.cpp):

    p_vertex_attrs = &vertex_attrs;
    p_face_attrs = &face_attrs;

TriMesh has the slots p_vertex_attrs, p_edge_attrs and p_face_attrs; TetMesh adds p_tet_attrs. Registering a collection is what lets the operations roll it back (see Rollback).

docs.title: Tuples and navigation
docs.text:
Code names an element of the mesh with a Tuple. A tuple holds a vertex, an edge and a face at once, and in 3D a tetrahedron as well: in TriMesh it is a global vertex id, a local edge id and a global face id; in TetMesh, a global vertex id, a local edge id, a local face id and a global tetrahedron id. The same tuple is read as a vertex, an edge, a face or a cell depending on what is asked of it: vid(m), eid(m), fid(m), and in 3D tid(m).

Navigation moves from a tuple to a neighbouring one by changing one of its parts and keeping the others:

Function Changes Keeps switch_vertex(m) the vertex, to the other end of the edge edge, face (and tetrahedron) switch_edge(m) the edge, to the other edge of the face at this vertex vertex, face (and tetrahedron) switch_face(m) 2D: the triangle, to the next one around the edge; 3D: the face, to the other face of the tetrahedron at this edge vertex, edge (and tetrahedron) switch_tetrahedron(m) 3D: the tetrahedron, to the one across the face vertex, edge, face

The steps that cross into another cell return an optional, empty on the boundary: TriMesh::Tuple::switch_face and TetMesh::Tuple::switch_tetrahedron. A TriMesh may be non-manifold: around an edge with more than two triangles, switch_face steps through them in the order of their ids, and switch_faces lists the others. The other endpoint of an edge is t.switch_vertex(m).vid(m); this is how shortest edge collapse reads the two ends of the edge it is asked to collapse:

    const size_t v1 = t.vid(*this);
    const size_t v2 = t.switch_vertex(*this).vid(*this);

Each cell carries a hash that every operation rewriting the cell increments, and a tuple stores the hash of its cell. t.is_valid(m) is false when the cell is removed or its hash has changed, so a tuple taken before an operation is recognised as stale after it. consolidate_mesh() renumbers the mesh and invalidates every tuple.

docs.title: The operations
docs.text: The figures show each operation before and after. The red vertex, the red edge, the darker face (and the darker tetrahedron in 3D) are the tuple: on the left the tuple the operation is called with, on the right the tuple its after hook receives, where the figure marks one.

docs.title: In 2D
docs.text:
Edge split (split_edge) adds a vertex on the edge and splits each triangle on it in two.

Edge collapse (collapse_edge) merges the two ends of the edge. The vertex the tuple points at is removed, the other end survives, and the triangles on the edge disappear. The default before hook refuses a collapse that fails the link condition, which would change the topology (set_use_link_condition(false) turns it off).

Edge swap (swap_edge) replaces the edge shared by two triangles with the other diagonal of the quadrilateral they form. The default before hook refuses an edge that is not shared by exactly two triangles, and one whose new diagonal is already an edge.

Vertex smoothing (smooth_vertex) moves a vertex and does not change the connectivity: the operation is all in its hooks.

Face split (split_face) adds a vertex inside a triangle and splits it in three.

docs.title: In 3D
docs.text:
Edge split (split_edge) adds a vertex on the edge and splits each tetrahedron around it in two.

Edge collapse (collapse_edge) merges the two ends of the edge; as in 2D, the tuple's vertex is removed and the other end survives.

Face swap and edge swap (swap_face, swap_edge). The 2-3 face swap replaces two tetrahedra sharing a face with three around a new edge; the 3-2 edge swap is its inverse, and replaces the three tetrahedra around an interior edge with two.

4-4 edge swap (swap_edge_44) replaces the four tetrahedra around an interior edge with four others around a new edge; there are two ways to do it.

5-6 edge swap (swap_edge_56) is the same for the five tetrahedra around an interior edge, which become six.

Vertex smoothing (smooth_vertex) moves a vertex, as in 2D. Face split (split_face) and tetrahedron split (split_tet) add a vertex inside a face or a tetrahedron.

The scheduler knows the operations by name: edge_split, edge_collapse, edge_swap, vertex_smooth and face_split in both dimensions, and in 3D also face_swap, edge_swap_44, edge_swap_56 and tet_split (see Scheduling).

docs.title: Hooks and invariants
docs.text:
An algorithm specializes the operations by overriding virtual functions of its mesh class. Each operation has a before hook and an after hook (split_edge_before and split_edge_after, collapse_edge_before and collapse_edge_after, smooth_before and smooth_after, and so on for every operation above), and every operation calls the same invariants. Each returns false to refuse the operation:

  1. Before hook, op_before(t): runs before anything changes. It checks whether the operation makes sense here and caches what the after hook will need, such as the positions of the two ends of an edge.
  2. The connectivity change. The operation saves the records of the vertices and cells it is about to rewrite, then rewrites them.
  3. After hook, op_after(t): runs on the new connectivity, with the tuple shown in the figures. It computes the attributes of the new or changed elements, such as the position of a new vertex, and may refuse the result.
  4. Invariants, invariants(cells): runs on the cells the operation created (for smoothing, the cells around the vertex) and checks the conditions every cell must satisfy.

If both pass, the operation commits; otherwise it is rolled back. This is the middle of TriMesh::split_edge (TriMesh.cpp):

    new_tris = get_one_ring_tris_for_vertex(new_vertex);
    start_protect_attributes();

    // roll back if not successful
    if (!split_edge_after(return_tuple) || !invariants(new_tris)) {
        // rollback topo
        // restore old v, t
        for (const auto& old_v : old_vertices) {
            m_vertex_connectivity[old_v.first] = old_v.second;
        }
        for (const auto& old_t : old_tris) {
            m_tri_connectivity[old_t.first] = old_t.second;
        }
        // erase new_vid new_fids
        m_vertex_connectivity[new_vid].m_conn_tris.clear();
        m_vertex_connectivity[new_vid].m_is_removed = true;
        for (size_t i = 0; i < fids.size(); ++i) {
            m_tri_connectivity[new_fids[i]].m_is_removed = true;
        }
        rollback_protected_attributes();
        return false;
    }

Shortest edge collapse shows the split between the parts. Its after hook places the surviving vertex (at the midpoint, or on a frozen or boundary endpoint), from positions its before hook cached. Its invariant is the envelope: every new triangle must stay close to the input surface (ShortestEdgeCollapse.cpp):

bool ShortestEdgeCollapse::invariants(const std::vector<Tuple>& new_tris)
{
    // First: it touches only boundary edges, and is far cheaper than the surface test.
    if (!m_boundary_envelope.boundary_edges_inside(*this, vertex_attrs, new_tris)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (m_has_envelope) {
        for (auto& t : new_tris) {
            std::array<Eigen::Vector3d, 3> tris;
            auto vs = oriented_tri_vertices(t);
            for (auto j = 0; j < 3; j++) tris[j] = vertex_attrs[vs[j].vid(*this)].pos;
            bool outside = m_envelope.is_outside(tris);
            if (outside) return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

The optimizer meshes of tetwild, triwild and simwild put their checks in the hooks instead. Their collapse evaluates, in its before hook, the cells it would create, and refuses when one would be inverted or would raise the worst energy around the edge; its after hook refuses when a surface face leaves the envelope (see Quality and Robust geometry).

In a parallel pass the scheduler may run an operation as a dry run first: the before hook and the checks that precede the first change run, and the operation stops there (see Scheduling). A before hook that only reads the mesh and writes per-thread caches works unchanged in both cases. One that writes to the mesh must skip the write in a dry run, when other threads read the same vertices without locks; dry_run() says when, and the optimizer's rounding checks it.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
When the after hook or the invariants refuse, the operation is undone, and the mesh is exactly as it was before it started:

  • Connectivity. The saved records of every vertex and cell the operation rewrote are written back, with their hashes, so tuples taken before the operation are valid again. The vertices and cells the operation created are marked removed.

  • Attributes. Between start_protect_attributes() and the decision, every entry of a registered collection that the code reaches through non-const access is copied, on first access, to a per-thread list; rollback_protected_attributes() writes those copies back. Reading through const access records nothing (AttributeCollection.hpp):

        T& operator[](size_t i)
    {
        if (recording.local()) {
            m_rollback_list.local().emplace(i, m_attributes[i]);
        }
        return m_attributes[i];
    }

What is not restored: anything written by the before hook, which runs before the protection starts, and any state outside the registered collections (member variables, caches, counters). So a before hook writes only what may stay written when the operation is refused (the optimizer's smoothing rounds the vertex's coordinates there, which is valid either way), and an after hook writes nothing outside the collections that a refusal would have to undo. Vertex smoothing changes no connectivity, so its rollback is the attribute part alone.

docs.text:

  • Writing an operation in the developer guide.
  • The API reference of TriMesh and TetMesh.

docs.title: Quality
docs.text: tetwild, triwild and simwild improve the shape of their elements after the embedding has produced a valid but badly shaped mesh. They measure the shape of an element with the AMIPS energy, and apply splits, collapses, swaps and smoothing until the worst element is good enough. This page describes the energy, the optimization loop, smoothing, what happens when the loop stops making progress, and the optional coarsening pass at the end. The loop is shared by the three components (and topological_offset), in TetOptimizerMesh.cpp and TriOptimizerMesh.cpp.

docs.title: The AMIPS energy
docs.text:
Let \(J\) be the Jacobian of the affine map that takes the regular element (the equilateral triangle, the regular tetrahedron) to the element. The AMIPS energy is

\[ E_{2D} = \frac{\operatorname{tr}(J^\top J)}{\det J}, \qquad E_{3D} = \frac{\operatorname{tr}(J^\top J)}{(\det J)^{2/3}}. \]

It does not depend on the element's size, position or rotation. Its minimum is the dimension: 2 for an equilateral triangle, 3 for a regular tetrahedron. It grows without bound as an element degenerates, and an inverted or flat element has no energy: the code stores a sentinel value instead, MAX_ENERGY (\(10^{50}\); in 3D the logs show its cube root, \(4.6 \cdot 10^{16}\)).

The energy is evaluated by expressions generated for the purpose, in src/wmtk/utils/AMIPS.cpp and AMIPS2D.cpp. The 3D mesh stores the cube of the energy per tetrahedron and falls back to rational arithmetic when the double result is out of range (AMIPS.h):

template <typename rational>
double AMIPS_energy_stable_p3(const std::array<double, 12>& T)
{
    auto res = AMIPS_energy(T);

    if (res < 1e8 && res > 2) {
        return std::pow(res, 3);
    } else {
        return AMIPS_energy_rational_p3<rational>(T);
    }
}

The max energy in the logs and the reports is the largest \(E\) over the mesh (in 3D, the cube root of the stored value).

docs.title: The target: stop_energy
docs.text: stop_energy is the target: the optimization stops when the max energy is below it. The default is 100 in tetwild and triwild, 10 in simwild. The same number is not the same target in 2D and 3D, because the floors differ: 100 is 50 times the 2D minimum and about 33 times the 3D one. simwild can set a different target per region with quality_field; the optimization then compares each element's energy with its own region's target.

docs.title: The optimization loop
docs.text:
Each iteration runs the four kinds of operation over the whole mesh:

  1. Split every edge longer than \(\tfrac43\,l\,s\), where \(l\) is the target edge length (length_rel times the bounding box diagonal) and \(s\) the sizing scalar of the edge (the mean of its endpoints', 1 unless refined).
  2. Collapse edges shorter than \(\tfrac45\,l\,s\). A collapse is refused if it inverts an element or raises the worst energy around the edge.
  3. Swap edges and faces: 3-2, 4-4, 5-6 and 2-3 in 3D, edge swaps in 2D. A swap is taken when it lowers the worst energy of the elements it replaces.
  4. Smooth every vertex (below).

By default (interleaved_smoothing) each topology pass is followed by its own smoothing pass (split and smooth, collapse and smooth, swap and smooth), and the iteration ends early once the max energy is below stop_energy. Before the first iteration, a collapse pass without the length limit and a swap pass remove what the embedding left redundant; after the last, a collapse and a swap pass run once more.

The loop stops when the max energy is below stop_energy and every vertex has double coordinates (see Robust geometry), or after max_iterations (80).

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
Smoothing moves one vertex at a time, keeping the connectivity. For an interior vertex it minimizes the sum of the AMIPS energies of the elements around it, over the vertex's position, with Newton's method: polysolve's dense Newton solver, at most 10 iterations, with a line search that refuses a step that would invert an element (SmoothVertex.hpp, solver.hpp).

A vertex on the tracked surface must also stay on the input. smoothing_mode chooses how:

  • projected (the default). Smooth as if the vertex were interior, then walk back towards its start, at \(t = 1, \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \dots\) of the step, projecting each candidate onto the input. The first projected candidate that inverts nothing and strictly lowers the worst incident element is taken; if none is, after project_line_search_steps (12) halvings, the vertex does not move. The vertex lands exactly on the input.
  • exact. Minimize, with the same Newton solver, the energy below, in which the distance to the input pulls the vertex back. The vertex rests at a small distance from the input, proportional to \(w\).

The energy of the exact mode, for a vertex at \(x\), is

\[ w \sum_{c \ni x} E(c) \;+\; (1 - w)\left(\frac{d(x)}{\varepsilon}\right)^2 , \]

where the sum runs over the elements around the vertex, \(d(x)\) is the distance to the input, taken with its true Hessian (zero in the directions along a flat part of the input, so the vertex slides freely there), and \(w\) is w_amips (\(10^{-4}\)).

Whatever the mode, the new position is kept only if every surface face around the vertex is still inside the envelope, no element around it is inverted (exact test), and the worst element around it is not worse than before. Otherwise the vertex stays where it was.

num_smoothing_passes sets the number of passes when smoothing is not interleaved. With threads, smoothing runs by colour classes of non-adjacent vertices (see Scheduling).

docs.title: When the energy stalls: stuck_refine_*
docs.text:
Splits, collapses, swaps and smoothing can reach a configuration none of them improves: a sliver whose edges are too short to split and whose collapse or swap would make something worse. The max energy then stops going down. After each iteration the loop checks for this with (TetOptimizerMesh.h):

    virtual bool optimization_stalled(double prev, double cur)
    {
        return (prev - cur) <= m_params.stuck_refine_stall_eps * (cur - optimization_stop_metric());
    }

that is, the last iteration improved the max energy by at most stuck_refine_stall_eps (0.1) of the distance still to cover to stop_energy. When it did, the loop refines around the worst elements:

  • It selects the worst elements: every element whose energy is above \(\min(\max(E_{\max}/100,\ \texttt{stop\_energy}),\ 100)\), or the stuck_refine_num_worst worst if that is positive.
  • It multiplies the sizing scalar of their vertices, and of stuck_refine_rings rings around them, by stuck_refine_factor (0.5), down to stuck_refine_min_scalar, and grades the change into the surroundings so that neighbouring sizings differ by at most stuck_refine_gradation. The smaller target length lets the next split pass refine there.
  • With stuck_refine_force_split (on), it also splits the longest edge of each worst element once, whatever its length.

stuck_refine_cooldown (1) skips that many iterations after a refinement before the next one, so the operations act on the new sizing first.

docs.title: The coarsening pass
docs.text:
The collapse in the loop judges a candidate on the geometry right after the collapse, before any smoothing, so the converged mesh keeps vertices it does not need. The optional coarsen_pass runs after the loop, and removes them without letting the max energy rise:

  • It takes each collapse without the quality check, smooths the vertices within coarsen_smooth_ring (1) of the merged vertex coarsen_local_smoothing_passes times (0 by default), and keeps the collapse only if the worst element in that region is no worse than before. Elements outside the region are untouched, so the max energy of the mesh cannot rise.
  • It alternates such a collapse pass with coarsen_global_smoothing_passes (1) ordinary smoothing passes, for at most coarsen_max_rounds (2) rounds, and stops early when a round accepts nothing.
  • coarsen_unbounded (on) lets it coarsen past the target edge length, as far as the energy allows. Off, it leaves edges of \(\tfrac45\,l\) and longer alone.

The pass trades run time for elements: it is off by default. With volume_history_output it is refused when coarsen_local_smoothing_passes is above 0.

docs.text:
• The tetwild, triwild and simwild tutorials, for the settings on real inputs.
  • OptimizerParameters.h, where every parameter of the loop is documented with the measurements behind its default.
  • Hu et al. 2018, Tetrahedral Meshing in the Wild, and Hu et al. 2019, TriWild.

docs.title: Regions
docs.text: A mesh with several materials, organs or parts carries them as regions: named sets of top-dimensional cells (tetrahedra in 3D, triangles in 2D). A cell may belong to several regions, where they overlap, or to none, in the background. simwild builds such meshes and edits them; triwild tags its triangles by input; topological_offset and manifold_extraction select regions to work on. All of them name regions the same way, and select them with the same small expression language.

docs.title: Tags
docs.text:
On a mesh that leaves or enters a component, regions are the tags attribute of the top-dimensional cells: a UInt8 matrix with one column per region, labelled with the region's name, and a 1 where the cell belongs to the region. A cell in no region is the background; components write it as a column of its own, labelled ambient. In Python (in-memory I/O):

mesh["cells"]["tetrahedron"]["attributes"] = {
    "tags": {
        "values": np.array([[1, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=np.uint8),
        "labels": ["region_a", "region_b"],
    },
}

In a .msh file, each region is a physical group. Inside a component, each cell holds the set of the ids of its regions, and the mesh maps names to ids.

Regions come from:

  • simwild on surfaces or curves: one region per input, named by input_names (otherwise tag_0, tag_1, ...). A cell belongs to an input's region if it is inside that input: by default the input's winding number at the cell's centroid decides. For surfaces, tag_from_winding_number off propagates membership across the arrangement instead, from the outside of the box, flipping each time a face of the input is crossed; every input must then be closed. split_connected_components makes one region per connected component of a file.
  • triwild: one region per input curve, with the triangles inside it by winding number.
  • A tagged mesh given as input (a .msh, or a mesh in memory): its columns are its regions.

docs.title: Expressions
docs.text:
Options that select cells take a boolean expression over region names:

Expression Selects the cells a in region a a & b in both a and b (their overlap) a | b in a, in b, or in both !a not in a (a | b) & !c in a or b, and not in c _ in no region !_ in at least one region

! binds tightest, then &, then |: a | b & c is a | (b & c). A name is made of letters, digits, _ and -. In a selection, a name the mesh does not have is reported with a warning and selects nothing; in replace_tags_out and tag_priority, a new name creates the region. The parser is in components/simwild/wmtk/components/simwild/expression_parser/.

The background depends on the component. simwild reads the ambient column as no region at all, so its background is _. topological_offset and manifold_extraction give the background a region of its own, named ambient, so there it is selected by that name.

docs.title: How components use them
docs.text:
Component Option Takes simwild, remeshing sizing_field a list of {"tags": expression, "length": ...} (or length_rel): a target edge length per selection; each cell takes the last entry that selects it, and each vertex the smallest length of its cells simwild, remeshing quality_field a list of {"tags": expression, "quality": ...}: a target energy per selection; where several apply, the last wins simwild, resolve_overlaps resolve_overlaps_tags pairs of expressions; each overlap is filled with the nearest of the two simwild, replace_tags replace_tags_in, replace_tags_out & only: the regions of each input expression are replaced by those of the output one simwild, fill_holes_topo, tight_seal_topo, keep_lcc fill_holes_tags, tight_seal_tag_sets, keep_lcc_tags & only: sets of regions simwild, tag_priority tag_priority region names, highest priority first topological_offset offset_selection an expression: the cells to offset; a single name selects single-body mode manifold_extraction tag_selection an expression: the cells whose boundary is made manifold

In simwild the surface the optimization tracks is the interface between regions: the faces whose two cells do not belong to the same regions. It is held in the envelope like tetwild's tracked surface, and it is what history_output records (see Histories).

docs.text:
• The simwild tutorial and the regions workflow.
  • The topological offset and manifold extraction tutorials.
  • In-memory I/O for the full description of mesh dictionaries and tags.

docs.title: Robust geometry
docs.text: The meshing components take inputs as they come: self-intersecting, open, non-manifold, degenerate. Three mechanisms keep their meshes valid on such inputs: vertices keep exact rational coordinates where doubles cannot represent them, every orientation test is exact, and an envelope bounds how far the surface may move from the input.

docs.title: Exact and rounded positions
docs.text:
The optimizer meshes (TriOptimizerMesh and TetOptimizerMesh, behind tetwild, triwild, simwild and topological_offset) keep each vertex position twice: as doubles (m_posf), which everything reads, and as rationals (GMP, wmtk::Rational), which the exact tests read. A flag, m_is_rounded, says which one is the vertex's position.

  • Where rationals come from. The embedding computes an exact arrangement of the input with a background mesh. A vertex where the input crosses itself or the background mesh has rational coordinates that are in general not doubles.
  • Rounding. A vertex is rounded when its rational position is replaced by its conversion to doubles. That happens only if no incident cell becomes inverted or flat; otherwise the vertex keeps its rational position. After the embedding, the vertices whose coordinates are already doubles are rounded at once, and every other vertex is tried.
  • During the optimization. Only an edge split creates a rational vertex: it places the new vertex at the midpoint in doubles, and if that inverts a cell, at the exact rational midpoint, which lies on the edge and cannot invert anything. Collapses, swaps and smoothing never un-round a vertex. A collapse tries to round the vertex it keeps, smoothing the vertex it moves, and a sweep tries every remaining rational vertex after each smoothing pass.
  • At the end. The optimization does not stop at its energy target while a vertex is still rational (the log says energy target reached, but ... vertices are still un-rounded; continuing). The output is written in doubles; tetwild logs Not all vertices rounded! when the run ends with rational vertices left. simwild's stop_at_float stops as soon as every vertex is rounded, regardless of the energy.

Rounding a vertex in 3D is this (TetOptimizerMesh.cpp, two lines for dry runs left out):

bool TetOptimizerMesh::round(const Tuple& v)
{
    size_t i = v.vid(*this);
    if (m_vertex_attribute[i].m_is_rounded) return true;

    const auto old_exact = m_vertex_attribute[i].m_exact;
    m_vertex_attribute[i].set_pos_to_posf();
    auto conn_tets = get_one_ring_tets_for_vertex(v);
    m_vertex_attribute[i].m_is_rounded = true;
    for (auto& tet : conn_tets) {
        if (is_inverted(tet)) {
            m_vertex_attribute[i].m_is_rounded = false;
            m_vertex_attribute[i].m_exact = old_exact;
            return false;
        }
    }

    return true;
}

The rational copy is stored only while it differs from the doubles (ExactPosition.hpp), so a rounded vertex costs nothing extra.

docs.title: Exact predicates
docs.text:
Every decision about orientation is exact:

  • Orientation tests (orient2d, orient3d in src/wmtk/utils/predicates.hpp) use Marco Attene's Indirect_Predicates: a floating-point filter answers when it can decide the sign, and exact arithmetic answers when it cannot.
  • Inversion. A cell whose vertices are all rounded is tested with orient3d (or orient2d) on the doubles; a cell with a rational vertex is tested by computing the determinant in rational arithmetic. A flat cell counts as inverted.
  • Quality. In 3D, the AMIPS energy of a tetrahedron is computed in doubles when all its vertices are rounded and the result is in the range doubles evaluate reliably, and in rational arithmetic otherwise. In 2D it is computed in doubles.
  • Smoothing refuses any Newton step that would invert a cell around the vertex, by the same orientation tests.

The arrangement that creates the rational vertices is itself exact; see Embedding.

docs.title: Envelopes
docs.text:
The envelope is the set of points within distance \(\varepsilon\) of the input. The meshing components keep their tracked surface (or, in 2D, their tracked curves) inside it: an operation that creates or moves a surface face checks the new faces, and is refused if one leaves the envelope. The envelope bounds how far the output strays from the input. It does not bound the converse: a part of the input the output no longer covers is not detected by it.

\(\varepsilon\) is set relative to the input. eps_rel is a fraction of the diagonal of the input's bounding box, \(\varepsilon = \texttt{eps\_rel} \cdot \text{diag}\), and the target edge length length_rel is relative to the same diagonal. simwild also takes absolute values, eps and length.

tetwild builds the main envelope around the original input, at \(\varepsilon\), and the other envelopes it needs as fractions of it: the input simplification runs inside simplify_envelope_ratio \(\cdot\,\varepsilon\) (0.5), so the optimizer starts with room to move; open boundaries and non-manifold edges stay in a tube of order2_envelope_ratio \(\cdot\,\varepsilon\); feature curves in one of feature_envelope_ratio \(\cdot\,\varepsilon\). With several inputs, each tracked face is held to the envelopes of the inputs it lies on, not only to the envelope of all of them together.

docs.title: The containment test: exact or sampled
docs.text:
Whether a triangle (or a segment) lies inside the envelope is decided by one of two tests. Both answer the same question about the same envelope: they are given the same \(\varepsilon\), and neither is wider than the other. They differ in how they answer.

  • Exact (the default). The test of fast-envelope (Wang et al. 2020, Exact and Efficient Polyhedral Envelope Containment Check), decided with exact predicates. It has three versions: for triangles in 3D, for segments in 3D, and for segments in 2D.
  • Sampled (use_sample_envelope). Points are laid on the query: a lattice of spacing \(\varepsilon\) on a triangle, evenly spaced points less than \(\varepsilon\) apart on a segment. Each point is tested against the input through a bounding-volume hierarchy. Since the test cannot see between two points, it accepts a point only within a radius smaller than \(\varepsilon\), reduced by the distance from any point of the query to the nearest sample: \(\varepsilon - \varepsilon/\sqrt{3}\) for the lattice on a triangle, \(\varepsilon/2\) for points on a segment. If every sample passes, every point of the query is within \(\varepsilon\).

The reduced radius is the sampled test's own conservatism, not a smaller envelope. Its cost is that the sampled test refuses some geometry that is inside the envelope. Its purpose is speed: on some inputs the exact test dominates the run time. The two tests disagree on geometry close to the envelope's boundary, so switching from one to the other changes the output.

The radii, from Envelope.cpp, where _eps is the envelope's \(\varepsilon\) (eps2 and eps2_edge are the squared radii the samples are tested against):

    sampling_dist = _eps;
    const double real_envelope = _eps - _eps / std::sqrt(3);
    eps2 = real_envelope * real_envelope;
    // Edge queries sample a line, not a lattice; see eps2_edge in the header.
    const double real_envelope_edge = _eps - _eps / 2;
    eps2_edge = real_envelope_edge * real_envelope_edge;

tetwild, triwild and simwild also have simplify_use_sample_envelope, which switches the test for the input simplification only.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Embedding: where the rational coordinates come from.
  • Quality: what the operations optimize inside the envelope.
  • The QSlim tutorial measures how the envelope limits a simplification.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text: An algorithm decides which operations to attempt and in which order; the toolkit runs them. A pass takes a list of candidate operations, each a name and a tuple, and runs them through a priority queue: it attempts the most urgent, queues the new candidates each success creates, and stops when the queue is empty or a stopping criterion says so. The class that runs a pass is wmtk::ExecutePass<Mesh>, in src/wmtk/ExecutionScheduler.hpp. The algorithm configures it with callbacks; how the operations are spread over threads is hidden from it.

docs.title: A pass
docs.text:
Shortest edge collapse (Hoppe 1996) is one pass: collapse every edge, shortest first, until the mesh is down to a target number of vertices. Its candidates are all the edges (ShortestEdgeCollapse.cpp):

    auto collect_all_ops = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, Tuple>>();
    for (auto& loc : get_edges()) collect_all_ops.emplace_back("edge_collapse", loc);

and the pass is configured and run like this (the renew callback returns an edge_collapse for every edge of the triangles the collapse left around the surviving vertex):

    auto measure_len2 = [](auto& m, auto op, const Tuple& new_e) {
        auto len2 =
            (m.vertex_attrs[new_e.vid(m)].pos - m.vertex_attrs[new_e.switch_vertex(m).vid(m)].pos)
                .squaredNorm();
        return -len2;
    };
    auto setup_and_execute = [&](auto& executor) {
        executor.num_threads = NUM_THREADS;
        executor.renew_neighbor_tuples = renew;
        executor.priority = measure_len2;
        executor.stopping_criterion_checking_frequency =
            target_vert_number > 0 ? (initial_size - target_vert_number - 1)
                                   : std::numeric_limits<int>::max();
        executor.stopping_criterion = [](auto& m) { return true; };
        executor(*this, collect_all_ops);
    };

    if (NUM_THREADS > 0) {
        auto executor = wmtk::ExecutePass<ShortestEdgeCollapse>(ExecutionPolicy::kPartition);
        executor.lock_vertices = [](auto& m, const auto& e, int task_id) {
            return m.try_set_edge_mutex_two_ring(e, task_id);
        };
        setup_and_execute(executor);
    } else {
        auto executor = wmtk::ExecutePass<ShortestEdgeCollapse>(ExecutionPolicy::kSeq);
        setup_and_execute(executor);
    }

The operation itself (collapse_edge, with its hooks and invariants) is the local operation; the pass only decides when to attempt it.

docs.title: The callbacks
docs.text:
Member What it decides edit_operation_maps The operations by name. The constructor registers edge_split, edge_collapse, edge_swap, vertex_smooth and face_split, and on a TetMesh also face_swap, edge_swap_44, edge_swap_56 and tet_split. priority(m, op, t) A number per candidate; the largest is attempted first. Shortest edge collapse returns minus the squared length, so the shortest edge comes first. renew_neighbor_tuples(m, op, new_tuples) After a success, the new candidates, from the tuples the operation returned. should_renew(priority) Whether a renewed candidate is queued at all. is_weight_up_to_date(m, (priority, op, t)) Whether a popped candidate still holds. A candidate is queued with the priority it had then; the mesh around it may have changed since, and this drops it if so. lock_vertices(m, t, task_id) Parallel passes only: claim the vertices the operation needs (see below). stopping_criterion(m), stopping_criterion_checking_frequency When to stop before the queue is empty. on_fail(m, op, t) Called for a refused operation, for a driver that collects failures to retry.

The loop pops the candidate with the largest priority, skips it if its tuple is no longer valid or is_weight_up_to_date rejects it, attempts the operation, and on success queues what renew_neighbor_tuples returns with their priorities. Ties are broken by the operation's name and the tuple, so a serial pass pops candidates in the same order every time.

stopping_criterion_checking_frequency is a threshold, not a period: once the pass has had that many successful operations, stopping_criterion is consulted after every operation. Shortest edge collapse and QSlim set it to the number of collapses that reaches the target vertex count, with a criterion that always says stop, so the pass ends on the collapse that reaches the target. The passes of tetwild, triwild and simwild have no stopping criterion: each runs until its queue is empty, and the optimization loop around them decides when to stop (see Quality).

A pass that refuses an operation does not attempt it again. The optimizer passes run the executor repeatedly until nothing succeeds, re-offering a failed operation only when a successful one changed a vertex around it (LocalizedRetry.hpp).

docs.title: Parallel passes
docs.text:
The policy picks the execution: ExecutionPolicy::kSeq runs one queue on one thread; ExecutionPolicy::kPartition runs the pass on num_threads threads. Every component chooses kSeq when num_threads is 0 and kPartition otherwise.

Partitions. The mesh's vertices are divided into partitions. The optimizer meshes of tetwild, triwild and simwild sort them by the Morton code of their positions and cut the order into num_threads parts; with more than one thread, shortest edge collapse makes four partitions per thread, so that a thread that drew light ones goes on to take more. Each candidate goes to the queue of the partition of its tuple's vertex. Each thread takes a partition no other thread has taken, drains its queue in priority order, and takes the next one. The priority order therefore holds within a partition, not across the mesh.

Locks. Before an operation runs, its thread claims the vertices around the tuple with lock_vertices: one mutex per vertex, acquired with a try-lock that never waits. A topology change claims the two-ring of its edge, smoothing the one-ring of its vertex; an operation that reads further asks for more (the coarsening pass claims one ring more than it smooths). Two operations whose claims overlap cannot run at the same time; all the others can. An operation that loses the race for a lock is set aside and retried after other work of the same thread; after max_retry_limit attempts (10) it goes to a queue that is drained serially once every thread has finished.

Screening. Most attempted operations are refused by their first checks: on tetwild's hard models about 98% are refused before they change anything. So a parallel pass runs in rounds, and each round first dry-runs every candidate in parallel, without locks, against the unchanged mesh: the before hook and the checks before the first change run, and the operation stops there. Only the candidates that survive take locks and are attempted for real, with every check repeated. Serial passes are not screened, nor is a pass with a stopping criterion; the 2D collapse pass of the optimizer turns screening off, because it costs more than it saves there.

Smoothing by colour. In tetwild, triwild and simwild, parallel vertex smoothing uses no locks by default (colored_smoothing): the vertices are divided into classes of pairwise non-adjacent vertices, and the classes are smoothed one after another, each class entirely in parallel. Two vertices of a class share no cell, so neither writes what the other reads.

Storage. The storage of vertices and cells cannot grow while threads run on it: it grows only at serial points, between operations of a serial pass and between the rounds of a parallel one, where each thread gets a budget of new slots for the next round.

The threads are the toolkit's own pool, built on std::thread (src/wmtk/threading/). The workers are started once and reused from pass to pass.

docs.title: Threads and determinism
docs.text:
Every component that has a num_threads option defaults it to 0.

  • num_threads 0 runs every pass serially, with a single queue that pops in a fixed order. The same input and options give the same output from run to run, on the same build and machine.
  • num_threads 1 runs the parallel scheduler on one thread: another code path (partitions, screening rounds), so another result than 0, though the same one from run to run.
  • num_threads 2 or more: the order in which operations run depends on which thread wins which lock, and an operation that changes the mesh changes what the next ones see, so the result changes slightly from run to run. It also depends on the number of threads, which sets the partitions. Colour-class smoothing alone does not depend on the number of threads.

tetwild on sphere.obj from data/models, with default options, run twice per setting:

num_threads Output vertices, two runs Identical outputs 0 9,504 and 9,504 yes 1 9,511 and 9,511 yes 4 9,509 and 9,479 no

The QSlim tutorial measures the speed-up from 1 to 8 threads and the spread of the result on another model. For comparisons between runs, for bug reports and for regression tests, use num_threads 0.

docs.text:

  • Writing an operation and the Wild driver in the developer guide.
