docs.title: Developer guide
docs.text:
These pages are for changing the toolkit: fixing a component, adding an operation or a component, or working on the core library. They describe the code as it is on main, with links to the source.

  • The life of a component call: from wmtk_app -j or a Python call to the component's mesh and back.
  • The Wild driver: the optimization loop that tetwild, triwild, simwild and topological_offset share.
  • Writing an operation: the hooks, invariants and rollback, on the shortest edge collapse component.
  • Writing a component: the checklist.
  • Testing: what the test suites check and how CI runs them.
  • Writing documentation: this site, its examples and its generated reference.
  • Contributing: formatting, pull requests, the data repository.

The design notes go deeper on single subjects: component I/O, tracking, and what simwild adopted from tetwild and triwild.

docs.title: The repository
docs.text:
Directory What it holds src/wmtk/ The library, CMake target wmtk::toolkit: the meshes, the scheduler, envelopes, I/O, histories. components/ One directory per component, and the CMake functions that register them (components/cmake/). app/ wmtk_app, the command line, and the headers CMake generates for it. python/ The wildmeshing package: the bindings (python/src) and its pure-Python part (python/wildmeshing). tests/ The library's Catch2 tests, the integration test driver, the Python tests. docs/ This site: pages, examples (docs/examples), the reference generator (docs/tools). cmake/ One recipe per dependency (cmake/recipes/, most of them CPM), and the data pin. data/ The clone of the data repository. Not part of this repository (.gitignore).

The top-level CMakeLists.txt adds src/wmtk, then app, python/src (with WMTK_PYBIND, on by default), tests (with BUILD_TESTING), and components last: registering a component links it into wmtk_app, the Python module and the integration tests, which must exist by then.

docs.title: The library: src/wmtk
docs.text:
The core files, at the top of src/wmtk:

File What it is TriMesh.h, TriMesh.cpp The triangle mesh: connectivity, Tuple navigation, the local operations (split, collapse, swap, smooth, face split) with their _before / _after hooks, rollback, locks, consolidation. TetMesh.h, TetMesh*.cpp The same for tetrahedra; each operation's connectivity change has its own file (TetMeshEdgeCollapsingConn.cpp, TetMeshSwapMeshConnectivity.cpp, ...), and TetMeshTriangleInsertionConn.cpp / TetMeshCutTable.cpp insert triangles into a tet mesh. TriOptimizerMesh.h, TriOptimizerMesh*.cpp What triwild, simwild-2D and topological_offset-2D share: vertex, edge and face attributes, the split / collapse / swap / smooth passes and the optimization loop. See the Wild driver. TetOptimizerMesh.h, TetOptimizerMesh*.cpp The 3D counterpart, for tetwild, simwild-3D and topological_offset-3D. OptimizerParameters.h The parameters of the optimizer meshes, with the measurements behind their defaults. ExecutionScheduler.hpp ExecutePass: the priority queues, the locks, the serial (kSeq) and partitioned parallel (kPartition) policies. See scheduling. AttributeCollection.hpp Per-simplex attributes, with the thread-local record that rollback restores. SlotPool.hpp The preallocated connectivity storage and the atomic counter that hands out fresh slots to parallel operations. MeshData.hpp MeshData, MeshMap and ComponentResult: the meshes the memory route takes and returns. OperationDryRun.hpp The thread-local dry-run flag the scheduler's screening uses. RationalPositions.h, ExactPosition.hpp Vertex positions kept both as doubles and, while a vertex cannot be rounded, as rationals. SurfaceTagAttributes.h Whether a face (3D) or edge (2D) is tracked surface, and which bounding-box side it is on. Types.hpp The Eigen and rational types used throughout.

And the subdirectories:

Directory What it holds envelope/ Envelope (exact, through fast-envelope, or sampled), BoundaryEnvelope (a tube around an open boundary), union and intersection envelopes, KNN. history/ The recorded histories of a run, their file format and replay. See tracking. io/ ComponentIO (the file and memory routes of a component), mesh readers and writers (read_mesh / write_mesh), VTU writers. optimization/ AMIPS and envelope energies and the vertex smoother, on polysolve. simplex/ Simplices named by their vertices, and collections of them. threading/ The toolkit's own task pool, parallel_for, concurrent queues, vertex mutexes and enumerable_thread_specific. utils/ Everything else: exact predicates, Delaunay and the VolumeRemesher embedding, partitioning, sizing-field helpers, winding numbers, run_pass and the localized retry loop, logging.

docs.title: Components, the app and the bindings
docs.text:
Each component lives in components/<name>/wmtk/components/<name>/: its entry points <name>.hpp / <name>.cpp, its mesh class, its options (<name>_spec.json) and its tests (tests/). Writing a component lists what a new one needs.

wmtk_app (app/main.cpp) and the Python module (python/src/pywildmeshing.cpp) know the components only through headers that CMake writes into app/ at configure time: the life of a component call follows one call through them.

docs.title: Tests and data
docs.text:
tests/ holds the library's unit tests (wmtk_tests), the integration test driver (integration_tests.cpp) and the Python tests (tests/python); each component's own tests are in its tests/ directory. Testing describes them all.

The meshes and the integration configs are in the data repository. When tests are enabled, the build clones it into data/ (CMake's ExternalProject, target wmtk_data_download), at the commit pinned by GIT_TAG in cmake/wmtk_data.cmake. Tests read it through the WMTK_DATA_DIR definition of the wmtk::data target. A build with BUILD_TESTING=OFF, as the Python package's, does not clone it.

docs.title: Where to start reading
docs.text:
1. ShortestEdgeCollapse.cpp: the smallest complete use of a mesh, an operation and the scheduler, walked through in writing an operation.
  2. TriMesh.h, for Tuple and the hooks, and TriMesh::collapse_edge in TriMesh.cpp, for the order in which an operation calls them.
  3. ExecutePass in ExecutionScheduler.hpp: its members are the callbacks a pass sets.
  4. TriOptimizerMesh::mesh_improvement in TriOptimizerMesh.cpp, then the Wild driver, before touching tetwild, triwild, simwild or topological_offset.

docs.title: The life of a component call
docs.text: A component is a pair of C++ functions in wmtk::components::<name>. wmtk_app, the Python module, the integration tests and C++ programs all call one of the two. This page follows a call from the command line to the component's mesh and back, with shortest edge collapse as the example.

docs.title: The two entry points
docs.text:
Every component declares both, in wmtk/components/<name>/<name>.hpp:

namespace wmtk::components::shortest_edge_collapse {

void shortest_edge_collapse(nlohmann::json json_params);
ComponentResult shortest_edge_collapse(nlohmann::json json_params, const MeshMap& meshes);

}

The first is the file route: inputs and outputs are files named in the options. The second is the memory route: inputs are entries of meshes, nothing is written, and the outputs come back as a ComponentResult, a pair of named output meshes and a JSON report (src/wmtk/MeshData.hpp). Both build an io::ComponentIO and call the same run():

void shortest_edge_collapse(nlohmann::json json_params)
{
    io::ComponentIO context;
    run(std::move(json_params), context);
}
ComponentResult shortest_edge_collapse(nlohmann::json json_params, const MeshMap& meshes)
{
    io::ComponentIO context(&meshes);
    run(std::move(json_params), context);
    return context.take_result();
}

docs.title: How the callers find the components
docs.text:
wmtk_app and the bindings name no component in their code. add_component(<name>) (components/cmake/add_component.cmake) appends one line per component to six headers in app/, which components/CMakeLists.txt empties at the start of every configure:

Header The line it gets Included by components_include.hpp #include <wmtk/components/<name>/<name>.hpp> wmtk_app, the bindings, the integration tests components_map.hpp components_map["<name>"] = the file overload wmtk_app, the bindings, the integration tests components_memory_map.hpp memory_components["<name>"] = the memory overload the bindings components_spec_include.hpp #include <<name>_spec.hpp> wmtk_app, the bindings components_spec_map.hpp components_spec_map["<name>"] = the spec's accessor wmtk_app, the bindings components_python.hpp WMTK_PYTHON_BINDINGS(<name>), only if python/src/<name>_bindings.cpp exists the bindings

The maps are filled where the headers are included, inside a function:

std::map<std::string, std::function<void(nlohmann::json)>> components_map;
// include auto-generated map
#include "components_map.hpp"

The headers are generated: edit add_component, not them, and reconfigure after adding a component. add_component also links the component into wmtk_app, into the Python module (with WMTK_PYBIND) and into wmtk_integration_tests (with WMTK_BUILD_INTEGRATION_TESTS).

docs.title: wmtk_app
docs.text:
app/main.cpp takes three options: -j <file>, --list and --options <name>. With -j it

  1. parses the JSON file, and requires an application key;
  2. removes $schema (an editor's, see JSON Schemas), and sets input_dir to the directory of the JSON file, so that the component resolves the paths in the file against it;
  3. looks the application up in components_map (Application ... unknown otherwise);
  4. warns about every top-level key the component's spec does not have (see below);
  5. calls the file overload with the JSON.

main does not catch what the component throws: a component fails with log_and_throw_error, which logs the message, and the process ends on the uncaught exception.

docs.title: Inside the component
docs.text:
run() takes the same steps in every component.

1. The route. component_io.prepare(json_params, "<name>") does nothing on the file route. On the memory route it sets application, empties input_dir, output, log_file and report, and, for simwild, tetwild and triwild, wraps a single input string into a list.

2. Validation and defaults. The component checks the JSON against its spec and fills in the defaults:

const auto spec =
    jse::embed::wmtk_shortest_edge_collapse_spec::shortest_edge_collapse_spec::spec();
jse::JSE spec_engine;
bool r = spec_engine.verify_json(json_params, spec);
if (!r) {
    log_and_throw_error(spec_engine.log2str());
}
json_params = spec_engine.inject_defaults(json_params, spec);

The spec is compiled in: add_component runs jse_add_spec on <name>_spec.json, which generates <name>_spec.hpp, declaring the accessor above, and a source file holding the JSON, both in generated/<name>/ in the build directory. The json-spec-engine checks types, required keys and allowed values; with strict off, its default, it accepts keys no rule covers, and the component then never reads them. Only topological_offset sets spec_engine.strict = true and refuses them. tetwild, triwild and simwild do this step through utils::verify_and_setup_logger (src/wmtk/utils/DriverPrologue.hpp), which also opens log_file.

3. The inputs. component_io.path(root, json_params["input"]) is the file path, resolved against input_dir by utils::resolve_path (against the current directory when input_dir is empty), on the file route, and the mesh's name on the memory route. component_io.triangles(...) then reads the file, or takes the named MeshData and checks its attributes, and cleans both the same way: duplicate vertices (within remove_duplicate_eps), degenerate faces and unreferenced vertices go.

4. The mesh. The component builds its own mesh class from the arrays:

ShortestEdgeCollapse m(v, num_threads, !use_sample_envelope);
wmtk::set_preallocation_factor_from_json(m, json_params);
m.set_use_link_condition(use_link_condition);
m.create_mesh(v.size(), tri, modified_v, envelope_size, boundary_envelope_size);

5. The operation loop. Here m.collapse_shortest(target_verts), which runs one ExecutePass over every edge (writing an operation). tetwild, triwild, simwild and topological_offset run mesh_improvement() (the Wild driver).

6. The output. consolidate_mesh() compacts the mesh; the file route writes output (when it is not empty: the memory route emptied it); the memory route fills component_io.result:

if (component_io.memory())
    component_io.result.first["mesh"] =
        io::triangle_data(m, [&](size_t v) { return m.vertex_attrs[v].pos; });
component_io.result.second = {
    {"vertices", m.get_vertices().size()},
    {"triangles", m.get_faces().size()}};

docs.title: The memory route
docs.text:
io::ComponentIO (src/wmtk/io/ComponentIO.hpp) is the only place that knows which route a call is on (memory()); the rest of the component asks it for inputs and hands it outputs. On the memory route:

  • A selector ("input": "surface") names an entry of the MeshMap. A missing one throws Unknown input mesh; every one is validate()d; an attribute the component does not accept throws Unknown mesh attribute.
  • Nothing is written. A recorded history goes into the report as bytes (save_history, then take_result() puts it under "history", and a volume history under "volume_history").
  • The component logs to a console logger of its own, not to a file logger the caller set up.

On both routes, ComponentIO holds a process-wide mutex for the duration of the call: component calls in one process run one at a time.

The contract of each component's inputs, the MeshData layout and the NumPy dictionaries are specified in component I/O.

docs.title: The Python bindings
docs.text:
The module wildmeshing._core is built from python/src/pywildmeshing.cpp and mesh_conversion.cpp; python/wildmeshing/__init__.py re-exports it. For every component in memory_components, the module defines one function with two overloads:

  • wm.<name>(options, meshes): the memory route. call_component (mesh_conversion.cpp) converts the meshes the selectors name (the keys input, input_edges, input_points, surface_mesh, uv_mesh, envelope, tet_mesh, output_tet_mesh and features), releases the GIL, calls the memory overload and returns (outputs, report) as NumPy dictionaries.
  • wm.<name>(options): the file route, as wmtk_app runs it. It adds application if it is missing and releases the GIL. It does not set input_dir, so relative paths resolve against the current directory.

The docstring of each function is built from its spec, as wmtk_app --options prints it: help(wm.qslim) lists every option. Next to the components:

  • wm.components(): the names of the components, from the spec map.
  • wm.spec(name): a component's spec, the rules of its *_spec.json, as a Python list.
  • wm.wildmeshing(options) and wm.wildmeshing(options, meshes): dispatch on options["application"], for code written against the older single entry point.

A component with Python classes or functions of its own puts them in python/src/<name>_bindings.cpp, defining wmtk::python::bind_<name>(module); add_component compiles the file into the module and lists it in components_python.hpp, and the module calls it. simwild and tracking have one.

docs.title: The spec map
docs.text:
app/component_specs.hpp reads the specs for wmtk_app and the bindings: the root rule's doc (the rule with pointer /), the top-level options in the spec's order, each option's type, default and the first sentence of its doc.

wmtk_app --list prints every component with the first sentence of its root doc. wmtk_app --options <name> prints the root doc, the URL of the component's reference page, and one line per option:

$ wmtk_app --options shortest_edge_collapse
shortest_edge_collapse

Simplifies a triangle mesh by collapsing its shortest edges first (Hoppe 1996, Progressive Meshes), until the vertex count reaches the target. With a positive eps_rel, every collapse keeps the surface inside an envelope around the input.

Options (every one, with its full description: https://wildmeshing.github.io/wildmeshing-toolkit/reference/shortest_edge_collapse/):
  application (string, required): Application name must be shortest_edge_collapse.
  input (string, required): Triangular input mesh.
  output (string, default "out.obj"): Output file name (with extension).
  ...

So a spec's root doc should open with a sentence that says what the component does, and each option's doc with a sentence that stands alone. The full text of each doc goes into the reference (writing documentation).

docs.title: Unknown options
docs.text:
Since most components ignore a key their spec does not have, a misspelled option would silently keep its default. component_specs::unknown_options lists the top-level keys that are not options of the spec (input_dir and $schema excepted), and the callers warn about each:

  • wmtk_app: tetwild has no option `eps_rell` (wmtk_app --options tetwild lists them).
  • The bindings, on both overloads of wm.<name> and of wm.wildmeshing: tetwild has no option `eps_rell` (see help(wildmeshing.tetwild)).

The warning does not stop the run, and a direct C++ call does not warn. topological_offset, with its strict validation, then refuses the key.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Changes reach main through pull requests on GitHub. This page covers what a pull request needs to pass, and the two places a change can reach outside the code: the documentation and the data repository. CONTRIBUTING.md at the root of the repository is the short version.

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
C and C++ code is formatted with clang-format, by the rules in .clang-format (based on Google's style, 4-space indents, 100 columns). .pre-commit-config.yaml pins the version, clang-format 21.1.8 from mirrors-clang-format, and applies it to C, C++ and CUDA files. Install the hook once, and every commit formats the files it changes:

pip install pre-commit
pre-commit install
pre-commit run --all-files      # the whole tree, as CI checks it

.github/workflows/pre-commit.yml runs the same hook on every pull request and every push to main, and fails on any file it would change. Another clang-format version can format the same code differently: format with the pinned one, through pre-commit, rather than with the one an editor bundles.

Python, CMake and JSON files have no formatter in the hooks; follow the file around the change.

docs.title: Pull requests
docs.text:
• Work on a branch of your own, by convention <user>/<topic> (uday/offset-carry-correspondence).
  • Open the pull request against main. Say what changes and why; for a change that moves results, give the before and after on the models it affects (element counts, energies, times), and keep the description current as commits are added.
  • main is protected. A pull request can be merged when these checks pass: Linux (Debug), Linux (Release), macos-latest (Debug), macos-latest (Release), Windows 2025 (VS 2026) (Debug), Windows 2025 (VS 2026) (Release) (the jobs of continuous.yml, see testing) and pre-commit. The Linux arm64 jobs run as well, and are not required.
  • The branch must be up to date with main before it merges: merge main into it when another pull request lands first, and let the checks run again.
  • Pull requests are merged with a merge commit, and the branch is deleted.

Before opening one:

  • [ ] The code is formatted (pre-commit run --all-files).
  • [ ] New tests are registered: ctest --test-dir build -N lists them (testing).
  • [ ] The tests pass in Debug and in Release; a change to a component also runs its integration configs (-DWMTK_BUILD_INTEGRATION_TESTS=ON).
  • [ ] A new or changed option is documented in its spec, and python docs/tools/gen_reference.py --check passes.
  • [ ] The pages that describe the change are updated, and mkdocs build --strict passes.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site is built from docs/ and from the components' specs; writing documentation describes how. On every pull request, .github/workflows/docs.yml runs gen_reference.py --check and mkdocs build --strict, and uploads the built site as the artifact docs-preview; on main it deploys it. What a change to the code asks of the site:

  • An option is documented by its doc in the spec, and nowhere else: the reference, wmtk_app --options and the Python docstrings are generated from it. Changing an option's meaning or default means changing its doc.
  • A behaviour a tutorial describes (a default, a number a tutorial measured, an output field) means updating the tutorial, and rerunning its examples when the numbers come from them.
  • An example under docs/examples is built and run with -DWMTK_BUILD_DOC_EXAMPLES=ON, which the Release jobs of continuous.yml set; run them locally first (ctest --test-dir build -R doc_example), in a Release build.
  • A new component gets an entry in docs/components.yml and a tutorial (writing a component).

docs.title: The data repository
docs.text:
The meshes and integration configs live in data2. The build clones it into data/ (or the directory in the WMTK_DATA_ROOT cache variable) and checks out the commit pinned in cmake/wmtk_data.cmake:

GIT_REPOSITORY https://github.com/wildmeshing/data2.git
# ...
GIT_TAG 89911f53375f21eb6e8463caaca5bf07ce9c22c7

data/ is a clone checked out at that commit, a detached HEAD. To change the data:

  1. Make a branch in data2, from data/ or a clone of your own, and add the models and configs. A config is listed in integration_tests/integration_tests.json to run in CI; one in a group of its own (challenging_low_stop_energy_models.json, topological_offset_models.json, manifold_extraction_models.json) runs only when its hidden test case is asked for (testing).
  2. Open a pull request on data2 and merge it.
  3. In the toolkit's pull request that needs the data, set GIT_TAG to the data2 commit, and add a line to the log in the comment above it: the commit, the date, the data2 pull request or branch, and what changed for which config. The log is the history of the pin: read it before moving it.

A config that changes in data2 changes what CI runs only when the pin moves, so a pull request that needs new data, or new values in a config, carries the pin bump. Reconfigure and build to check the new pin out in data/.

Keep models small: every CI job of every pull request clones the whole repository, and every Release job runs the listed configs.

docs.title: Writing documentation
docs.text: The site is MkDocs with the Material theme, built from docs/ by mkdocs.yml. Everything on it is either written in docs/ or generated from the code on every build; nothing generated is committed.

docs.title: Building the site
docs.text:
pip install -r docs/requirements.txt
mkdocs serve            # http://127.0.0.1:8000, rebuilt on every change
mkdocs build --strict   # as CI does: a broken link or anchor fails the build

CI (.github/workflows/docs.yml) builds the site with --strict on every pull request and deploys it from main, with the Doxygen C++ reference under /api/.

docs.title: What is generated
docs.text:
docs/tools/gen_reference.py reads every components/<name>/wmtk/components/<name>/<name>_spec.json and docs/components.yml, and writes, at build time:

  • reference/<name>.md: every option of the component, with its type, default and doc. The options in key_options (components.yml) come first; DEBUG_, EXPERIMENTAL_ and TESTING_ options are folded away. Each option has an anchor: link to one as ../reference/tetwild.md#eps_rel.
  • reference/<name>_defaults.json: the options that have a default, with it.
  • schemas/<name>.json and schemas/wmtk_app.json: JSON Schemas for editors (see JSON Schemas).
  • The reference's navigation: a new component appears on its own.

So the spec is the documentation of an option: improve an option's description by editing its doc in the spec, and help(wildmeshing.<name>), wmtk_app --options <name> and the reference change with it. gen_reference.py --check (run in CI) fails when a rule has no doc, when a spec has no entry in components.yml, or when an entry names an option its spec does not have.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Every example on the site is a file under docs/examples/, included into pages, built and run by the tests. A page never contains example code of its own that is not in one of these files.

Directory What How it is tested docs/examples/json/<name>.json a wmtk_app input file copied into a directory with the meshes it names, run with wmtk_app -j docs/examples/python/<name>.py a script run with python <name>.py in a directory of its own docs/examples/cpp/<name>.cpp a program built as wmtk_doc_example_<name>, linking every component, and run

All three are registered in ctest when CMake runs with -DWMTK_BUILD_DOC_EXAMPLES=ON (and BUILD_TESTING), in Release builds only: doc_example_cpp_<name> for each program, and doc_examples_python_json for the scripts and JSON files together (tests/python/test_docs_examples.py).

Conventions, so that the files run the same from the repository root, in the tests and on a reader's machine:

  • Input meshes come from data/models (the data repository, cloned by CMake when tests are enabled). Python and C++ read the directory from the environment variable WMTK_DATA, defaulting to data/models, so they run from the repository root as they are:

    DATA = Path(os.environ.get("WMTK_DATA", "data/models"))

    const char* env = std::getenv("WMTK_DATA");
const std::filesystem::path data = env ? env : "data/models";

    A JSON file names its meshes by file name alone ("input": "bunny.obj"): wmtk_app resolves input paths against the JSON file's directory (and writes outputs to the working directory), and the test copies the meshes there and runs in it. - Outputs go to the working directory, under names that say what they are (bunny_remeshed.msh). - Small and fast: an example takes seconds, a minute at most in Release. Pick a small mesh and options that keep the run short; a tutorial explains what to change for quality. - Sections: mark the part a page shows with snippet markers, and include it by name:

    outputs, report = wm.qslim(...)

    octocat = wm.read_mesh(str(DATA / "Octocat.obj"))
outputs, report = wm.qslim(
    {"input": "octocat", "target_rel": 0.1, "eps_rel": 0.002, "num_threads": 4},
    {"octocat": octocat},
)
simplified = outputs["mesh"]
print(len(octocat["V"]), "->", len(simplified["V"]), "vertices")

    A section name may not start with a digit ([start:2d] fails the build; [start:two_d] works). Inside a fenced block on the page, with the language set (```python). Paths are relative to the repository root. Including a whole file (--8<-- "docs/examples/json/qslim.json") is right for JSON. - An example with a test of its own starts with # docs-example: tested by <test file>, and test_docs_examples.py skips it (the tracking tutorial's pipeline is one: tests/python/test_tracking_correspondences.py).

Run them while writing:

cmake -B build -DWMTK_BUILD_DOC_EXAMPLES=ON ...
cmake --build build --target wmtk_doc_example_qslim wmtk_app wildmeshing
ctest --test-dir build -R 'doc_example' --output-on-failure

docs.title: Renderings
docs.text:
Pages show meshes in an interactive viewer, <wmtk-viewer> (docs/viewer, three.js, loaded on every page): the input on the left, the output on the right, one camera; tet meshes with a cut plane; cells colored by quality or by region. A page shows a gallery example by its id:

<div>
<wmtk-viewer example="qslim"></wmtk-viewer>
</div>

The examples are listed in docs/gallery/examples.yaml. Each runs a tutorial's JSON example (json: qslim), a component on meshes of data/models (component, inputs, options), or a pipeline, a function of docs/gallery/scenes.py that runs a workflow's script and returns the meshes to show. docs/tools/build_gallery.py runs them through the Python bindings and writes their assets to docs/gallery/assets/<id>/ (not committed: CI builds them, cached by the code they depend on); --posters also takes a still of each, used before the viewer starts and in the README. The gallery page is generated from the same list. To preview locally:

PYTHONPATH=build/bin python docs/tools/build_gallery.py qslim --posters
mkdocs serve

build_gallery.py --check (in CI) fails when a page names an example the list does not have. The viewer's source is docs/viewer/src/wmtk-viewer.js; after changing it, rebuild the bundle (npm install && npm run build in docs/viewer) and commit docs/assets/viewer/wmtk-viewer.min.js. Keep the input on the left and the output on the right in every figure.

docs.title: A tutorial page
docs.text:
One page per component, docs/tutorials/<name>.md, in this order:

  1. What it does, in a paragraph, and when to use it (and when another component fits better).

  2. A first run, in three tabs over the same run, with the same options:

    === "Command line"

    ```json
    {
      "application": "qslim",
      "input": "Octocat.obj",
      "output": "octocat_qslim.obj",
      "target_rel": 0.1,
      "eps_rel": 0.002,
      "num_threads": 4
    }

    ```

    ```bash
    wmtk_app -j qslim.json
    ```

=== "Python"

    ```python
    octocat = wm.read_mesh(str(DATA / "Octocat.obj"))
    outputs, report = wm.qslim(
        {"input": "octocat", "target_rel": 0.1, "eps_rel": 0.002, "num_threads": 4},
        {"octocat": octocat},
    )
    simplified = outputs["mesh"]
    print(len(octocat["V"]), "->", len(simplified["V"]), "vertices")
    ```

=== "C++"

    ```cpp
    wmtk::MeshMap meshes{{"octocat", wmtk::io::read_mesh(data / "Octocat.obj")}};
    auto [outputs, report] = wmtk::components::qslim::qslim(
        {{"input", "octocat"}, {"target_rel", 0.1}, {"eps_rel", 0.002}, {"num_threads", 4}},
        meshes);
    const wmtk::MeshData& simplified = outputs.at("mesh");
    std::cout << meshes.at("octocat").V.rows() << " -> " << simplified.V.rows() << " vertices\n";
    wmtk::io::write_mesh("octocat_qslim.msh", simplified);
    ```

    The tabs are linked across the site (content.tabs.link): a reader who picks Python sees Python everywhere. 3. Key settings: the options in the component's key_options, each with what it changes and when to change it, a link to its reference entry, and the numbers a reader needs (what the default does on the example, what a coarser or finer value gives). Measure them: run the example and say what came out. 4. Outputs: the files written, the fields on the mesh, what the report holds. 5. Recipes and pitfalls: what goes wrong in practice and what to do. 6. See also: the reference page, related tutorials, the paper.

Write in plain declarative sentences, present tense, without marketing. Numbers come from runs, not from memory: if a page says "about 1,000 faces", an example produced it.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The suites in the table are registered with ctest; the few that are not are run by hand, as the sections below say. A test that is built but not registered never runs, in CI or locally: after adding one, check that ctest --test-dir build -N lists it.

Suite Source ctest entries Registered when Library unit tests the files of TEST_SOURCES in tests/ one per test case BUILD_TESTING (on by default) Component unit tests components/<name>/.../tests/ wmtk_test_<name>, one per component BUILD_TESTING and WMTK_COMPONENT_TESTS (both on by default) Memory route tests/test_component_io.cpp one per test case as the component tests Integration tests tests/integration_tests.cpp, configs in data/integration_tests Integration_Tests WMTK_BUILD_INTEGRATION_TESTS=ON Python tests/python/ python_memory_io, python_tracking, python_tracking_correspondences the Python module is built and its interpreter has NumPy; the last in non-Debug builds only Documentation examples docs/examples/ doc_example_cpp_<name>, doc_examples_python_json WMTK_BUILD_DOC_EXAMPLES=ON, non-Debug builds only

docs.title: Library unit tests
docs.text:
wmtk_tests is one Catch2 executable built from the files listed in TEST_SOURCES in tests/CMakeLists.txt: a new test file goes into that list. catch_discover_tests registers every test case as a ctest entry of its own, under its name. The tests link wmtk::data, so they read the data repository through WMTK_DATA_DIR:

const std::string root(WMTK_DATA_DIR);

Small meshes built in code are in src/wmtk/utils/examples/ (TriMesh_examples.hpp: single_triangle(), two_triangles(), ...).

-DWMTK_DEBUG_BRUTE_FORCE_OPS=ON compiles a check into TriMesh's split and collapse that compares each result with one rebuilt from the whole mesh. It makes every operation linear in the mesh size: for tests on small meshes only.

docs.title: Component unit tests
docs.text:
Each component's tests/CMakeLists.txt calls add_component_test(<name>) (components/cmake/add_component_test.cmake), which builds wmtk_test_<name> and registers it as one ctest entry:

add_test(NAME ${COMPONENT_TEST_NAME} COMMAND ${COMPONENT_TEST_NAME} --allow-running-no-tests --durations yes)

--durations yes prints the time of every case, which is how a case too slow for the Debug jobs shows up in the CI log. To run one case, run the executable with its name or a tag:

ctest --test-dir build -R wmtk_test_qslim --output-on-failure
build/components/qslim/wmtk/components/qslim/tests/wmtk_test_qslim "[boundary]"

wmtk_component_io_tests (tests/test_component_io.cpp, built from components/CMakeLists.txt) tests the memory route: components called on named meshes, and the memory and file routes giving the same result. Each component's cases are compiled only when the component is (#ifdef WMTK_TEST_<name>).

docs.title: Integration tests
docs.text:
With -DWMTK_BUILD_INTEGRATION_TESTS=ON, wmtk_integration_tests (tests/integration_tests.cpp) runs every config listed in data/integration_tests/integration_tests.json, the way wmtk_app does (the JSON, input_dir set to its directory, the component from the generated map):

for (const auto& input_file : input_files) {
    const path& f = integration_tests_dir / input_file;
    CHECK(fs::exists(f));
    CHECK_NOTHROW(wmtk_wrapper(f));
}

That is the whole check: a config passes if it runs without throwing. No output is compared with a stored one. A config therefore asks its component to throw when the result is wrong: throw_on_fail (the output misses what the component promises: the target vertex count, the stop energy), max_expected_iterations in tetwild and triwild (more optimization iterations than expected), throw_on_nonconvergence in topological_offset. All the configs run in one ctest entry, Integration_Tests, with a timeout of 7200 s.

The other cases in the file are hidden ([.]): Catch2 does not run them unless asked, and catch_discover_tests does not register them. Each reads its own list from data/integration_tests:

build/tests/wmtk_integration_tests "[challenging]"   # challenging_low_stop_energy_models.json: minutes to hours each
build/tests/wmtk_integration_tests "[offset]"        # topological_offset_models.json
build/tests/wmtk_integration_tests "[manifold]"      # manifold_extraction_models.json

A new config goes into the data repository and its list, and the data pin moves to the data2 commit that has it (writing a component).

docs.title: Python tests
docs.text:
The tests in tests/python run the bindings. Three are registered in tests/CMakeLists.txt, when the module is built (WMTK_PYBIND, on by default) and the interpreter CMake found imports NumPy:

ctest entry File What it runs python_memory_io test_memory_io.py the memory route through the bindings, NumPy only python_tracking test_tracking.py histories as bytes and files, wm.Tracking, wm.CurveTracking, wm.VolumeTracking python_tracking_correspondences test_tracking_correspondences.py the tracking tutorial's pipeline (docs/examples/python/tracking_correspondences.py): the dense bunny remeshed, tetrahedralized, and every vertex mapped through both histories and back; its counts are ranges, since a run with threads changes slightly from one run to the next; non-Debug builds only, timeout 1800 s

The others are run by hand or elsewhere:

  • test_docs_examples.py: the documentation's examples, below.
  • test_smoke.py: imports the module and its error paths; the wheel builds run it with test_memory_io.py and test_tracking.py on every wheel (test-command in pyproject.toml).
  • test_integration.py: the integration configs through the bindings, compared byte for byte with wmtk_app's output when the config is serial (python -m pytest tests/python; see its README.md).

python/tests holds the tests of wildmeshing.polyfem_ops, run with python -m pytest python/tests and gmsh installed.

docs.title: Documentation examples
docs.text: With -DWMTK_BUILD_DOC_EXAMPLES=ON, every docs/examples/cpp/<name>.cpp is built as wmtk_doc_example_<name>, linked with every component, and in a non-Debug build registered as doc_example_cpp_<name>; doc_examples_python_json (tests/python/test_docs_examples.py) runs the Python scripts and, through wmtk_app -j, the JSON files. They check that each example runs without an error. Writing documentation has the conventions.

docs.title: Slow cases
docs.text:
Debug builds run 10 to over 100 times slower than Release. A case that takes more than a fraction of a second in Debug is tagged release_only: hidden in Debug builds, run as usual in Release. The pattern, at the top of the test file:

// Cases too slow for the Debug CI jobs, Windows Debug above all: Release builds only.
#ifdef NDEBUG
const std::string release_only = "";
#else
const std::string release_only = "[.]";
#endif

and on each slow case:

TEST_CASE("sec-open-surface-boundary-is-preserved", "[test_sec][boundary]" + release_only)

Commit e8494ffb4f introduced it for the 95 cases over 0.3 s in a macOS Debug build or 5 s on Windows Debug, taking a macOS Debug ctest to 27.5 s; tetwild's and simwild's whole runs were already hidden in Debug. A case that should not run anywhere by default, a benchmark on a large model say, gets a hidden tag of its own ([.slow]), and the reason in a comment.

docs.title: Running the tests locally
docs.text:
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DWMTK_BUILD_INTEGRATION_TESTS=ON
cmake --build build -j
ctest --test-dir build -N                                   # what is registered
ctest --test-dir build -E Integration_Tests --output-on-failure
ctest --test-dir build -R Integration_Tests --output-on-failure

The first build clones the data repository into data/.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
.github/workflows/continuous.yml runs on every pull request and every push to main, in eight jobs:

Job (check name) Runner Configs Linux ubuntu-latest Debug, Release Linux arm64 ubuntu-24.04-arm Debug, Release macos-latest macos-latest Debug, Release Windows 2025 (VS 2026) windows-2025-vs2026 Debug, Release

A check is named after its job and config, as in Linux (Release).

Each job configures with CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE set to its config, builds with two jobs (make -j2; Ninja on Windows) behind a compiler cache (ccache; sccache on Windows), and runs ctest --verbose --output-on-failure, one test at a time (CTEST_PARALLEL_LEVEL: 1). So:

  • every job runs the library, component and memory-route tests, with the release_only cases in the Release jobs only;
  • the Release jobs add -DWMTK_BUILD_INTEGRATION_TESTS=ON and -DWMTK_BUILD_DOC_EXAMPLES=ON, and run every listed integration config and the documentation's C++ examples;
  • the Linux jobs install python3-numpy, so they run the registered Python tests, and in Release the Python and JSON examples; the other jobs run them if the interpreter CMake finds has NumPy.

When the tests fail on Linux or macOS, a last step re-runs the component test executables under gdb or lldb and prints the backtrace of every thread, for a crash that leaves only a signal in the log. A manual run of the workflow (workflow_dispatch) with the debug_ssh input opens an SSH session on a Linux or macOS runner when a step fails.

Two other workflows run on every pull request: pre-commit.yml checks the formatting (contributing), and docs.yml checks the specs (gen_reference.py --check) and builds the site with --strict (writing documentation).

docs.title: The Wild driver
docs.text: tetwild, triwild, simwild and topological_offset improve their meshes with the same loop of splits, collapses, swaps and smoothing, written once per dimension: TetOptimizerMesh for tet meshes and TriOptimizerMesh for triangle meshes. Each component derives its mesh from one of them, inherits the passes and the loop, and changes what it needs through virtual hooks. This page describes the loop as the code runs it; the measurements behind the defaults are in the comments of OptimizerParameters.h.

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text:
Component Mesh class Base What runs the loop tetwild TetWildMesh TetOptimizerMesh mesh_improvement(max_iterations), after the input is simplified and embedded; use_legacy_code runs the older mesh_improvement_legacy instead triwild TriWildMesh TriOptimizerMesh mesh_improvement(max_iterations) simwild SimWildMesh (3D), SimWildMeshTri (2D) TetOptimizerMesh, TriOptimizerMesh mesh_improvement(max_iterations), for the operation remeshing topological_offset TopoOffsetTetMesh, TopoOffsetTriMesh TetOptimizerMesh, TriOptimizerMesh its own turns of local_operations() while it places the offset front, then mesh_improvement() for the final quality pass

The two bases are deliberately separate: the same algorithms on different primitives, with a different quality convention (a tet stores AMIPS cubed and the 3D loop reports its cube root; a triangle stores the 2D AMIPS energy). The header comment of each base says why it was seeded by moving tetwild's (3D) and triwild's (2D) implementation into it.

docs.title: The loop: mesh_improvement()
docs.text:
TetOptimizerMesh::mesh_improvement in TetOptimizerMesh.cpp, with logging and debug output left out; the 2D loop in TriOptimizerMesh.cpp is the same, without optimization_iteration_done():

compute_vertex_partition_morton();

if (optimization_bare_coarsen_passes()) {
    // Performing swaps after the initial collapse improves quality and convergence.
    local_operations({{0, 1, 1, 0}}, false);
}

double pre_max_metric = std::get<0>(optimization_quality_stats());
int refine_cooldown = m_params.stuck_refine_cooldown;

for (int it = 0; it < max_its; ++it) {
    if (!m_params.interleaved_smoothing) {
        std::tie(max_metric, avg_metric) =
            local_operations({{1, 1, 1, m_params.num_smoothing_passes}});
    } else {
        const int k = m_params.interleaved_smoothing_passes;
        const std::array<std::array<int, 4>, 3> passes = {
            {{{1, 0, 0, k}}, {{0, 1, 0, k}}, {{0, 0, 1, k}}}};
        for (const auto& ops : passes) {
            std::tie(max_metric, avg_metric) = local_operations(ops);
            if (max_metric < optimization_stop_metric()) break;
        }
    }
    optimization_iteration_done(it);

    // count the rounded vertices: cnt_round of cnt_verts
    if (max_metric < optimization_stop_metric()) {
        if (cnt_round == cnt_verts) break;
    }

    consolidate_mesh();

    if (optimization_stop_at_float() && round_and_check_all_rounded()) {
        break;
    }

    if (refine_cooldown > 0) {
        --refine_cooldown;
    } else if (
        it > 0 && max_metric > optimization_stop_metric() &&
        optimization_stalled(pre_max_metric, max_metric)) {
        refine_sizing_around_worst(max_metric);
        refine_cooldown = m_params.stuck_refine_cooldown;
    }
    pre_max_metric = max_metric;
}

if (optimization_bare_coarsen_passes()) {
    local_operations({{0, 1, 1, 0}});
}

coarsen_mesh();

The partition. At the start, the vertices are cut into NUM_THREADS parts along a Morton order of their positions; a parallel pass queues every operation in the part of its tuple's vertex (see scheduling). With num_threads 0 there is no partition, and every pass is serial.

The bare passes. Before the loop, a collapse pass without the length gate (collapse_limit_length false), then a swap pass: they remove what the embedding left. After the loop, a collapse pass with the gate, then a swap pass. When optimization_bare_coarsen_passes() returns false, neither runs. topological_offset's 2D mesh returns false; its 3D mesh returns true only under TetWild's rules, in its final pass. The offset surface is what its loop places, no envelope holds it, and an ungated collapse pass would decimate it (TetOptimizerMesh.h has the measurement).

An iteration. With interleaved_smoothing (on by default in all four components), three groups: splits, collapses, swaps, each followed by interleaved_smoothing_passes smoothing passes, and the iteration ends early after a group that brings the metric under the stop. Without it, one group: splits, collapses and swaps, then num_smoothing_passes smoothing passes.

The stop. The loop ends when the max metric is under optimization_stop_metric() and every vertex is rounded to doubles, or after max_iterations. For tetwild and triwild the metric is the max AMIPS energy and the stop is stop_energy. simwild overrides both: its metric is each cell's quality relative to its region's target, and the stop is 1. With simwild's stop_at_float, optimization_stop_at_float() also ends the loop as soon as every vertex is rounded, and skips it when every vertex already is.

Consolidation. After every iteration that does not stop, consolidate_mesh() compacts the storage: ids change, and every tuple held across it is invalid.

Stuck refinement. When an iteration improved the max metric by at most stuck_refine_stall_eps times the distance still to cover, the mesh is stalled:

return (prev - cur) <= m_params.stuck_refine_stall_eps * (cur - optimization_stop_metric());

refine_sizing_around_worst(), which each application implements, then lowers the sizing field around the worst cells. tetwild's (TetWildMesh.cpp) picks the cells above a filter energy, marks the longest edge of each for a forced split in the next split pass (stuck_refine_force_split), multiplies the sizing scalar of their vertices (grown by stuck_refine_rings rings) by stuck_refine_factor, down to stuck_refine_min_scalar, and grades the result into its surroundings (stuck_refine_gradation). After a refinement, the next stuck_refine_cooldown iterations do not refine.

Coarsening. coarsen_mesh() returns at once unless coarsen_pass is set; it is not gated by the bare passes. Then, for at most coarsen_max_rounds rounds, it runs a collapse pass in coarsening mode, where a collapse is kept only if the worst cell in the region it touched is no worse than before, then coarsen_global_smoothing_passes smoothing passes; it stops after a round that collapses nothing.

docs.title: A group: local_operations()
docs.text:
local_operations(ops) takes four counts, {split, collapse, swap, smooth}, and runs, in this order:

Count What runs ops[0] split_all_edges(), that many times ops[1] collapse_all_edges(collapse_limit_length), that many times ops[2] the swaps, at most that many times, stopping after a pass that swaps nothing: swap_all_edges() in 2D, swap_all_edges_all() then swap_all_faces() in 3D ops[3] smooth_all_vertices(ops[3]), then round_all_vertices()

After each kind that ran it logs the max and average energy, runs the sanity checks when DEBUG_sanity_checks is set, and calls update_attributes() (in 3D, update_attributes_and_history()). If a pass ran out of preallocated slots (slots_exhausted()), it consolidates, which reclaims the slots of removed simplices and re-derives the storage from the live count, and runs the same kind again.

docs.title: The passes
docs.text:
The split, collapse and swap passes collect their candidates in parallel (parallel_collect_edge_ops, parallel_collect_face_ops). Every pass runs them through an ExecutePass built by run_pass (src/wmtk/utils/RunPass.hpp): kPartition with NUM_THREADS > 0, kSeq otherwise, with the lock of its kind. All but smoothing run through run_localized_to_convergence (LocalizedRetry.hpp): the executor runs again until a round succeeds nowhere, and a failed operation is retried only if one of its vertices was in the region a successful operation renewed during that round.

Pass Candidates Popped first Dropped from the queue when Lock split every edge, edge_split the longest its length changed since it was queued, or it is not due: shorter than 4/3 of the target length times the sizing (splitting_l2), and not a forced split edge two-ring collapse every edge, both ways, edge_collapse the shortest its length changed, or, with the length gate, it is longer than 4/5 of the target length times the sizing (collapsing_l2) edge two-ring swap, 2D every edge, edge_swap the largest drop in max energy (swap_weight) its drop changed, or is under 1e-5 edge two-ring swap, 3D every edge, as edge_swap, edge_swap_44 and edge_swap_56; then every face, face_swap the longest edge edge two-ring; face two-ring for face swaps smoothing every vertex; with skip_good_regions, only the vertices of cells whose energy is at least skip_good_regions_margin times the stop energy, and every tracked-surface vertex vertex one-ring, or none (colored)

The target length is length_rel times the bounding box diagonal (OptimizerParameters::init_lengths_from_diagonal); the sizing is the mean of the two endpoints' sizing scalars, which stuck refinement lowers.

Three details matter when changing a pass:

  • Longest-edge order. In a parallel split pass an edge that loses a lock race is set aside, and the thread moves on to shorter edges. must_wait makes a split wait while a longer due edge of one of its cells is still queued, so that the parallel pass splits in the order the serial one does (the comment in TriOptimizerMeshSplit.cpp has the measurements).
  • Screening. A parallel pass first dry-runs every candidate without locks, and only the survivors take their ring locks (writing an operation). The 2D collapse pass turns it off (executor.screen_before_commit = false), where it costs more than it saves.
  • Colored smoothing. With colored_smoothing (the default, except in topological_offset) and more than one thread, smoothing does not lock: the vertices are split into classes of pairwise non-adjacent vertices (utils::greedy_vertex_coloring), and each class runs in parallel. A smoothing hook may then write only its vertex and its own cells, and must read everything outside the vertex's star through const access; every smooth checks it and throws on the first offence. In 3D, check_surface_folds turns colored smoothing off.

docs.title: What an application overrides
docs.text:
The bases implement the operation hooks (split_edge_before, collapse_edge_after, ...) and call narrower virtual hooks from them; tetwild, triwild and simwild override only those. topological_offset also overrides the operation hooks themselves.

Hook Default Overridden by refine_sizing_around_worst(max) none (pure virtual) every application optimization_quality_stats(), optimization_stop_metric() max and average AMIPS; stop_energy simwild (relative quality, stop at 1) optimization_stop_at_float() false simwild (stop_at_float) optimization_bare_coarsen_passes() true topological_offset optimization_stalled(prev, cur) the stall test above none collapse_quality_allowed allowed when the removed vertex is not rounded, or the new cells are no worse than the ring they replace (in 2D also: under stop_energy) simwild, topological_offset swap_quality_allowed strict improvement of the max energy topological_offset collapse_before_vertex, collapse_after_vertex, split_after_vertex, ... accept, do nothing tetwild (features, open boundaries), simwild, topological_offset smoothing_energy_envelope(vid) 2D: the mesh's envelope for a surface vertex; 3D: none (pure virtual) tetwild, triwild, simwild-3D, topological_offset cell_quality(tid), set_cell_quality(tid, q) (3D) none (pure virtual): the cell attributes are the application's tetwild, simwild, topological_offset allow_surface_swap(), check_surface_topology() (3D) none (pure virtual) tetwild and simwild (their options of the same names), topological_offset

The headers list the rest, each with what it may and may not do.

docs.title: Changing the shared code
docs.text: A change to TriOptimizerMesh or TetOptimizerMesh changes four components at once, and tetwild and simwild also simplify their input with ShortestEdgeCollapse. Run the unit tests of all four (wmtk_test_tetwild, wmtk_test_triwild, wmtk_test_simwild, wmtk_test_topological_offset) and the integration configs in a Release build (testing). When simwild moved onto the bases, the rule was that tetwild's and triwild's output must not move where the copies disagreed, and simwild's could; simwild: behaviours adopted from tetwild / triwild records each place where it did.

docs.title: Writing a component
docs.text: A component is a directory under components/, a CMake call that registers it, and a spec that documents its options. Registered, it is a wmtk_app application, a Python function and a C++ library (wmtk::<name>) at once. This page is the checklist, in the order the work goes; the existing components are the examples, shortest edge collapse the smallest.

docs.title: 1. The directory
docs.text:
components/<name>/wmtk/components/<name>/
    CMakeLists.txt          add_component, the sources, the tests
    <name>_spec.json        the options
    <name>.hpp, <name>.cpp  the two entry points
    <Mesh>.h, <Mesh>.cpp    the mesh class, its hooks and its passes
    tests/
        CMakeLists.txt      add_component_test, the test sources
        test_<name>.cpp

The three <name> levels are what the include path needs: add_component adds components/<name> to the include directories, so the header is #include <wmtk/components/<name>/<name>.hpp>, as the generated headers write it.

docs.title: 2. CMake
docs.text:
The component's CMakeLists.txt, after shortest edge collapse's:

set(COMPONENT_NAME shortest_edge_collapse)
add_component(${COMPONENT_NAME})

if(NOT ${WMTK_ENABLE_COMPONENT_${COMPONENT_NAME}})
    return()
endif()

set(SRC_FILES
    ShortestEdgeCollapse.cpp
    ShortestEdgeCollapse.h
    shortest_edge_collapse.hpp
    shortest_edge_collapse.cpp
)

target_sources(wmtk_${COMPONENT_NAME} PRIVATE ${SRC_FILES})

target_link_libraries(wmtk_${COMPONENT_NAME} PUBLIC
    wmtk::toolkit
)

if(${WMTK_COMPONENT_TESTS})
    add_subdirectory(tests)
endif()

and one line in components/CMakeLists.txt:

add_subdirectory("<name>/wmtk/components/<name>")

add_component(<name>) (components/cmake/add_component.cmake) defines the option WMTK_ENABLE_COMPONENT_<name> (on), the library wmtk_<name> and its alias wmtk::<name>, embeds the spec (jse_add_spec), appends the component to the generated headers in app/, and links it into wmtk_app, the Python module and the integration tests (the life of a component call). Reconfigure after adding it: the headers are written at configure time.

A component that uses another links it, as tetwild and simwild link wmtk::shortest_edge_collapse to simplify their input.

docs.title: 3. The entry points
docs.text:
In <name>.hpp, in namespace wmtk::components::<name>, exactly these two signatures, which the generated maps take the address of:

void <name>(nlohmann::json json_params);
ComponentResult <name>(nlohmann::json json_params, const MeshMap& meshes);

Write one run(nlohmann::json, io::ComponentIO&) and call it from both, as every component does (the life of a component call). In run:

  • start with component_io.prepare(json_params, "<name>");
  • validate and inject the defaults with the embedded spec, jse::embed::wmtk_<name>_spec::<name>_spec::spec() (or utils::verify_and_setup_logger, which also opens log_file);
  • get every input through component_io (path, paths, triangles, edges, mesh), so the memory route reads the MeshMap and the file route the files;
  • on the memory route, put the output meshes in component_io.result.first and write no file; put what a caller may want to check (counts, energies, times) in the report, component_io.result.second;
  • throw with log_and_throw_error when the result is not what was asked for, at least when throw_on_fail is set: the integration tests only see exceptions.

The memory route's contract, input by input, is in component I/O; add the component's row to its table. If a mesh selector has a new name, add it to the list of keys call_component converts in python/src/mesh_conversion.cpp, or the Python memory route will not pass that mesh.

docs.title: 4. The spec
docs.text:
<name>_spec.json is a list of json-spec-engine rules. It is what validates the options, and it is their documentation: wmtk_app --options, help(wildmeshing.<name>), the reference and the JSON Schemas are all generated from it. The root rule names the required and optional keys and says what the component does:

{
  "doc": "Simplifies a triangle mesh by collapsing its shortest edges first (Hoppe 1996, Progressive Meshes), until the vertex count reaches the target. With a positive eps_rel, every collapse keeps the surface inside an envelope around the input.",
  "pointer": "/",
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["application", "input"],
  "optional": ["output", "input_dir", "num_threads", "target_rel", "eps_rel", "..."]
}

and every option has a rule of its own, with a doc:

{
  "pointer": "/target_rel",
  "type": "float",
  "default": 0.1,
  "doc": "Target number of vertices relative to input number."
}
  • The first sentence of the root doc is the component's line in wmtk_app --list; the first sentence of an option's doc is its line in --options. Make both stand alone.
  • Give every optional key a default; inject_defaults fills it in, and run can then read json_params["..."] without checking.
  • Every spec has application, with "options": ["<name>"]. Give it input_dir too, which wmtk_app sets, and, where they apply, the keys most components share: output, num_threads, log_file, report, throw_on_fail.
  • Options for diagnostics, unfinished work or the tests start with DEBUG_, EXPERIMENTAL_ or TESTING_: the reference folds them away.
  • A key the spec does not have is accepted and ignored (with a warning from wmtk_app and the bindings), unless the component sets spec_engine.strict = true. So do not read a key that is not in the spec.

python docs/tools/gen_reference.py --check fails when the root rule or any other rule has no doc, when the spec has no entry in docs/components.yml, or when that entry names an option the spec does not have, a group that does not exist or a tutorial that is not there.

docs.title: 5. Unit tests
docs.text:
tests/CMakeLists.txt:

if(NOT BUILD_TESTING)
    return()
endif()
if(NOT ${WMTK_ENABLE_COMPONENT_TEST_${COMPONENT_NAME}})
    return()
endif()

add_component_test(${COMPONENT_NAME})

set(SRC_FILES
    test_<name>.cpp
)
target_sources(wmtk_test_${COMPONENT_NAME} PRIVATE ${SRC_FILES})

add_component_test(<name>) (components/cmake/add_component_test.cmake) builds the Catch2 executable wmtk_test_<name>, linked with the component, wmtk::toolkit and wmtk::data (for WMTK_DATA_DIR), and registers it with ctest as one entry of the same name. A test executable that is built but not registered never runs, in CI or locally; check that it is:

ctest --test-dir build -N | grep wmtk_test_<name>

Tag the cases too slow for a Debug build release_only (testing). If the component has a memory route, add a case to tests/test_component_io.cpp under #ifdef WMTK_TEST_<name>, and the component to the list in components/CMakeLists.txt that links wmtk_component_io_tests and defines that macro.

docs.title: 6. An integration config
docs.text:
An integration test is a whole run from a JSON file in the data repository: integration_tests/<name>_<model>.json, with its paths relative to that directory ("input": "../models/Octocat.obj"). Reuse a model from models/ when one fits; add a small one otherwise. Set throw_on_fail (or the component's equivalent) so that a bad result fails the test, and keep the run short: every Release CI job runs every listed config.

  1. Add the config, and any new model, to data2, and list the config in integration_tests/integration_tests.json; open a pull request there.
  2. Once it is merged, set GIT_TAG in cmake/wmtk_data.cmake to the data2 commit, with a line in the comment above it saying what changed (contributing).

docs.title: 7. The documentation
docs.text:
1. An entry in docs/components.yml:

    shortest_edge_collapse:
  title: Shortest edge collapse
  group: surface
  tutorial: tutorials/shortest_edge_collapse.md
  key_options: [input, output, target_rel, eps_rel, boundary_eps_rel, use_link_condition, use_sample_envelope]
  papers:
    - "[Hoppe 1996, Progressive Meshes](https://hhoppe.com/pm.pdf)"

    group is one of the groups at the top of the file; the reference page of a wip component opens with a work-in-progress warning. The reference page and its place in the navigation are generated from this entry and the spec; key_options come first on it. 2. A tutorial, docs/tutorials/<name>.md, in the order writing documentation gives, and its entry in the nav of mkdocs.yml. 3. Its examples, docs/examples/{json,python,cpp}/<name>.*, which the tests build and run (writing documentation).

docs.title: 8. Python
docs.text: Nothing to do: the module defines wm.<name> with both overloads from the generated maps, and its docstring from the spec. Classes or functions of the component's own go in python/src/<name>_bindings.cpp, defining wmtk::python::bind_<name>(pybind11::module_&); add_component compiles the file when it exists (the life of a component call).

docs.title: Before the pull request
docs.text:
• [ ] wmtk_app --list shows the component, and wmtk_app --options <name> its options.
  • [ ] ctest --test-dir build -N lists wmtk_test_<name>, and it passes in Debug and Release.
  • [ ] python docs/tools/gen_reference.py --check reports no problems.
  • [ ] mkdocs build --strict builds, with the new tutorial.
  • [ ] The integration config runs with wmtk_app -j, and the data pin names the data2 commit that has it.
  • [ ] The code is formatted (contributing).

docs.title: Writing an operation
docs.text: The local operations themselves (split, collapse, swap, smoothing, ...) are written once, in TriMesh and TetMesh. An application customizes them by deriving a mesh class and overriding hooks: a _before and an _after per operation, and invariants. It then runs them with an ExecutePass, which decides the order and the parallelism. This page describes what the mesh calls and when, what a failed operation undoes, and then walks through the shortest edge collapse component, the smallest complete example. Local operations describes the operations themselves, and scheduling the scheduler.

docs.title: The order of the calls
docs.text:
TriMesh::collapse_edge (src/wmtk/TriMesh.cpp), with the debug checks and the bookkeeping left out:

bool TriMesh::collapse_edge(const Tuple& loc0, std::vector<Tuple>& new_tris)
{
    if (!collapse_edge_before(loc0)) {
        return false;
    }
    // ... refuse a collapse that would leave the surviving vertex without a face
    if (dry_run()) return true; // checks done, the change would come next

    collapse_edge_conn(loc0, new_tris, return_t, new_vid, old_tris, old_vertices, ...);

    start_protect_attributes();

    if (!collapse_edge_after(return_t) || !invariants(new_tris)) {
        collapse_edge_rollback(new_vid, old_tris, old_vertices, ...);
        rollback_protected_attributes();
        return false;
    }
    // ... commit the edit to the history, if one is recorded
    release_protect_attributes();
    return true;
}

Every operation of TriMesh and TetMesh has this shape:

  1. <op>_before(t) runs on the mesh as it is. It decides whether the operation is worth trying, and saves what _after will need: positions, flags, the energy before. Returning false ends the operation; nothing has changed.
  2. The mesh's own checks: a TriMesh swap refuses a boundary edge, a collapse one that would leave the surviving vertex without a face. The TriMesh link condition is the base collapse_edge_before itself (unless set_use_link_condition(false)): an override that wants it calls TriMesh::collapse_edge_before(t) first, as shortest edge collapse does.
  3. In a dry run the operation stops here and returns true (below).
  4. The connectivity changes, and the operation keeps what it needs to undo it. Some checks come with the change and can still refuse here: a TetMesh collapse tests the link condition and duplicate tets as it rewires them.
  5. Attribute protection starts: from here on, attribute writes are recorded.
  6. <op>_after(t) runs on the new connectivity. It sets the attributes of what the operation created or changed (the position of the new vertex, the quality of the new cells) and may still refuse: false rolls the operation back.
  7. invariants(cells) runs on the cells around the change; false rolls the operation back.
  8. On success the edit goes into the history, if one is recorded, and the attribute record is dropped.

The tuple _after receives depends on the operation. A TriMesh collapse keeps the second vertex of the edge (t.switch_vertex(m)) and removes the first, and collapse_edge_after gets a tuple at the surviving vertex. split_edge_after gets the half of the old edge at its first vertex: t.switch_vertex(m) is the new vertex. The comments in TriMesh.h and TetMesh.h describe the others.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text: invariants(const std::vector<Tuple>& cells) is called after every operation's _after, with the cells it created or changed: in a TriMesh, the triangles around the surviving vertex of a collapse, the one-ring of the new vertex of a split, the triangles of a swap, the one-ring of a smoothed vertex. It is the place for what every operation must keep (the surface inside its envelope, no inverted element), so that a new operation added to the class keeps it too. The default returns true.

docs.title: Thread-local caches
docs.text:
_before and _after are two calls, and in a parallel pass other threads run other operations in between on the same mesh object. What _before saves for _after therefore goes into a per-thread value, never a plain member:

struct PositionInfoCache
{
    Eigen::Vector3d v1p;
    Eigen::Vector3d v2p;
    // ...
};
wmtk::threading::enumerable_thread_specific<PositionInfoCache> position_cache;

position_cache.local() returns the calling thread's value, created on first use. An operation runs on one thread from _before to the end, so what that thread wrote in _before is what it reads in _after. enumerable_thread_specific is the toolkit's own (it replaced TBB's); it is neither copyable nor movable, and so neither is a mesh class that holds one.

docs.title: What rollback restores
docs.text:
When _after or invariants says no, the operation is undone:

  • The connectivity of every cell and vertex the operation changed, from the copies the connectivity step kept.
  • The attributes this thread reached through the non-const operator[] of a registered AttributeCollection, since start_protect_attributes(): each entry gets back the value it had at its first access. A collection is registered by pointing the mesh's p_vertex_attrs, p_edge_attrs, p_face_attrs (and, in a TetMesh, p_tet_attrs) at it, usually in the constructor; an AttributeContainerGroup registers several for one simplex type.

It does not restore:

  • what _before wrote to the mesh's attributes: protection starts after it. _before writes to its cache only.
  • members of the mesh class, counters, caches, and collections not registered.
  • the slots a split took: they stay used, marked removed, until the next consolidate_mesh().

Reading through the non-const operator[] also records the entry. Read with .at(i) or through a const reference: it copies nothing, and it keeps the record to what the operation wrote, which matters where the record is checked (colored smoothing throws if a smoothing hook wrote outside its vertex's star, see the Wild driver).

Set every field of a vertex the operation creates rather than relying on what its slot holds, as IsotropicRemeshing::split_edge_after does (va = VertexAttributes{}, then the fields).

docs.title: Locks
docs.text: In a parallel pass, the scheduler locks a region around the operation's tuple before calling it and releases it after: for the operations queued on edges, the vertices of the two-ring of the edge (try_set_edge_mutex_two_ring), for smoothing the one-ring of the vertex. The hooks may read and write only inside that region. An operation that reaches farther (one that smooths a ring of vertices inside a collapse, say) needs a lock of a larger radius: try_set_edge_mutex_n_ring(e, task_id, n), which run_pass (src/wmtk/utils/RunPass.hpp) uses when it is given a radius.

docs.title: Dry runs
docs.text:
A parallel ExecutePass with screen_before_commit (on by default) runs in rounds, and each round first dry-runs every candidate, in parallel and without locks (src/wmtk/OperationDryRun.hpp): the operation runs up to its first change and returns true. Only the candidates that pass are then tried for real, with their locks, every check repeated. So in a dry run _before runs concurrently with other _before calls on an unchanging mesh, without a lock, and may write only thread-local caches and atomic counters. A hook that has to write the mesh tests dry_run() and skips the write, answering as if it had succeeded. A counter in _before sees a candidate twice when it passes the dry run.

Serial passes and passes with a stopping criterion (shortest edge collapse and qslim with a target) are not screened.

docs.title: Running it: ExecutePass
docs.text:
ExecutePass<AppMesh> (src/wmtk/ExecutionScheduler.hpp) takes a list of (operation name, tuple) pairs and runs them in priority order. Its members are the rules of the pass:

Member What it decides Default edit_operation_maps the operation each name runs edge_split, edge_collapse, edge_swap, vertex_smooth, face_split; in a TetMesh also edge_swap_44, edge_swap_56, face_swap, tet_split priority(m, op, t) the order: the largest value is popped first 0 is_weight_up_to_date(m, elem) whether a popped entry still holds (its priority may be stale) true renew_neighbor_tuples(m, op, new_cells) what a success puts back in the queue nothing should_renew(priority) whether a renewed entry is queued true lock_vertices(m, t, task) the region a parallel operation locks; false if another thread holds part of it always succeeds stopping_criterion, stopping_criterion_checking_frequency when the pass stops early never on_fail(m, op, t) what to do with a failed operation nothing num_threads, the policy (kSeq, kPartition) serial, or one queue per partition of the mesh kSeq

An entry whose cell has changed since it was queued is dropped before it runs: a Tuple stores the hash its cell had when the tuple was made, an operation on the cell changes the cell's hash, and is_valid compares the two. With kPartition the mesh class must provide get_partition_id(const Tuple&).

docs.title: Worked example: shortest edge collapse
docs.text: ShortestEdgeCollapse simplifies a triangle mesh by collapsing its shortest edge first (Hoppe 1996), until it reaches a vertex count, optionally keeping the surface inside an envelope. It is one operation, the edge collapse, three hooks and one pass. tetwild and simwild also use it, to simplify their input surfaces, so a change here changes them too.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
struct VertexAttributes
{
    Eigen::Vector3d pos;
    size_t partition_id = 0;
    bool freeze = false;
    bool input_boundary = false;
};

class ShortestEdgeCollapse : public wmtk::TriMesh
{
public:
    wmtk::Envelope m_envelope;
    bool m_has_envelope = false;
    wmtk::BoundaryEnvelope m_boundary_envelope;
    wmtk::AttributeCollection<VertexAttributes> vertex_attrs;
    wmtk::AttributeCollection<FaceAttributes> face_attrs;
    // ...
};

The constructor registers both collections, so that rollback and consolidation reach them:

NUM_THREADS = (num_threads);
// ...
p_vertex_attrs = &vertex_attrs;
p_face_attrs = &face_attrs;

create_mesh() builds the connectivity (TriMesh::init), the envelope when eps > 0, and the partition (partition_mesh(): four parts per thread when there is more than one), and then holds the open boundary: with a positive boundary_eps a BoundaryEnvelope, a tube around the input's boundary edges; otherwise freeze_boundary() freezes every boundary vertex.

docs.title: collapse_edge_before
docs.text:
bool ShortestEdgeCollapse::collapse_edge_before(const Tuple& t)
{
    if (!TriMesh::collapse_edge_before(t)) return false;

    // v1 is removed by the collapse, v2 survives (TriMesh::collapse_edge_conn keeps vid2).
    const size_t v1 = t.vid(*this);
    const size_t v2 = t.switch_vertex(*this).vid(*this);
    auto& cache = position_cache.local();
    cache.v1_frozen = vertex_attrs[v1].freeze;
    cache.v2_frozen = vertex_attrs[v2].freeze;

    if (cache.v1_frozen && cache.v2_frozen) {
        return false;
    }

    cache.v1_input_boundary = vertex_attrs[v1].input_boundary;
    cache.v2_input_boundary = vertex_attrs[v2].input_boundary;
    cache.v1_on_boundary = wmtk::BoundaryEnvelope::on_input_boundary(*this, vertex_attrs, t);
    cache.v2_on_boundary =
        wmtk::BoundaryEnvelope::on_input_boundary(*this, vertex_attrs, t.switch_vertex(*this));

    cache.v1p = vertex_attrs[v1].pos;
    cache.v2p = vertex_attrs[v2].pos;
    return true;
}

It first asks the base for the link condition (the component's use_link_condition). Two frozen endpoints cannot merge without moving one of them, so it refuses those. Everything else it only reads, into the thread-local cache: the endpoints' positions and flags, read before the connectivity changes.

docs.title: collapse_edge_after
docs.text:
bool ShortestEdgeCollapse::collapse_edge_after(const TriMesh::Tuple& t)
{
    const auto& cache = position_cache.local();
    const Eigen::Vector3d p = cache.v1_frozen                                 ? cache.v1p
                              : cache.v2_frozen                               ? cache.v2p
                              : cache.v1_on_boundary && !cache.v2_on_boundary ? cache.v1p
                              : cache.v2_on_boundary && !cache.v1_on_boundary
                                  ? cache.v2p
                                  : (cache.v1p + cache.v2p) / 2.0;
    const size_t vid = t.vid(*this);
    vertex_attrs[vid].pos = p;
    vertex_attrs[vid].freeze = cache.v1_frozen || cache.v2_frozen;
    vertex_attrs[vid].input_boundary = cache.v1_input_boundary || cache.v2_input_boundary;

    return true;
}

t is at the surviving vertex. It goes to the frozen endpoint if one is frozen, to the boundary endpoint if exactly one is on the input's boundary, and to the midpoint otherwise; it takes over the frozen and boundary flags. The writes come after start_protect_attributes(), so a collapse that invariants refuses gets its vertex back where it was.

docs.title: invariants
docs.text:
bool ShortestEdgeCollapse::invariants(const std::vector<Tuple>& new_tris)
{
    // First: it touches only boundary edges, and is far cheaper than the surface test.
    if (!m_boundary_envelope.boundary_edges_inside(*this, vertex_attrs, new_tris)) {
        return false;
    }
    if (m_has_envelope) {
        for (auto& t : new_tris) {
            std::array<Eigen::Vector3d, 3> tris;
            auto vs = oriented_tri_vertices(t);
            for (auto j = 0; j < 3; j++) tris[j] = vertex_attrs[vs[j].vid(*this)].pos;
            bool outside = m_envelope.is_outside(tris);
            if (outside) return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

The triangles around the surviving vertex must keep their boundary edges in the boundary tube, when there is one, and must lie inside the envelope, when there is one. The surface test reads the positions through the non-const operator[], so the neighbours' entries are recorded too: harmless here, and what .at() would avoid.

docs.title: The pass: collapse_shortest
docs.text:
size_t initial_size = get_vertices().size();
auto collect_all_ops = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, Tuple>>();
for (auto& loc : get_edges()) collect_all_ops.emplace_back("edge_collapse", loc);

auto renew = [&](auto& m, auto op, auto& tris) {
    // ... progress logging, every 10 s
    auto edges = m.new_edges_after(tris);
    auto optup = std::vector<std::pair<std::string, Tuple>>();
    for (auto& e : edges) optup.emplace_back("edge_collapse", e);
    return optup;
};
auto measure_len2 = [](auto& m, auto op, const Tuple& new_e) {
    auto len2 =
        (m.vertex_attrs[new_e.vid(m)].pos - m.vertex_attrs[new_e.switch_vertex(m).vid(m)].pos)
            .squaredNorm();
    return -len2;
};
auto setup_and_execute = [&](auto& executor) {
    executor.num_threads = NUM_THREADS;
    executor.renew_neighbor_tuples = renew;
    executor.priority = measure_len2;
    executor.stopping_criterion_checking_frequency =
        target_vert_number > 0 ? (initial_size - target_vert_number - 1)
                               : std::numeric_limits<int>::max();
    executor.stopping_criterion = [](auto& m) { return true; };
    executor(*this, collect_all_ops);
};

if (NUM_THREADS > 0) {
    auto executor = wmtk::ExecutePass<ShortestEdgeCollapse>(ExecutionPolicy::kPartition);
    executor.lock_vertices = [](auto& m, const auto& e, int task_id) {
        return m.try_set_edge_mutex_two_ring(e, task_id);
    };
    setup_and_execute(executor);
} else {
    auto executor = wmtk::ExecutePass<ShortestEdgeCollapse>(ExecutionPolicy::kSeq);
    setup_and_execute(executor);
}
  • The candidates: every edge once, as edge_collapse, the name of TriMesh::collapse_edge in edit_operation_maps.
  • The priority: minus the squared length, so the shortest edge is popped first.
  • The renewal: after a collapse, the edges of the triangles around the surviving vertex go back in the queue with their new lengths (new_edges_after). The entries queued before for those triangles fail is_valid and are dropped.
  • The stop: the criterion returns true, so the pass stops the first time it is consulted, which is once the successes exceed stopping_criterion_checking_frequency: after initial_size - target_vert_number collapses, each of which removes one vertex (in a parallel pass, the operations already running finish). The comment on that member in ExecutionScheduler.hpp explains why it is a threshold and not a period. The live criterion also keeps the pass out of screening, so the collapses run in priority order up to the count.
  • The policy: with threads, one queue per partition (get_partition_id returns the vertex's partition_id), each operation locking the two-ring of its edge; without, one serial queue.

The component around it (shortest_edge_collapse.cpp) reads the options and the mesh, calls create_mesh and collapse_shortest, then consolidate_mesh() and the output, as the life of a component call describes.
